The use of these adjectives by these books further centers – albeit subtly and not immediately made clear – the expectation that the students and/or teachers are white descendants of Europeans. In stark contrast, Sound Innovations 

describes the instruments used in a Japanese Folk Song as “unusual” and the melody of an Arabic Folk Song as “exotic”. Vallance (1974) argues that this hidden curriculum, though, is still learned systematically even if not explicitly taught. 52 

Another instance of language creating a hidden curriculum is present in Sound Innovations . Line 109 in the student book is the tune “Michael, Row Your Boat Ashore” and it is labeled “African-American Spiritual” by the authors. The student book includes an instruction unique to this line of music that is not printed anywhere else in the book: “always play with a beautiful sound” (Sheldon et al., 2010, p. 204). It is curious and most likely entirely innocent that this instruction was printed on the only line in the book that is explicitly labeled by the authors as a piece of music created by African-Americans. However, the pairing of this instruction on this line gives the impression that, were we to play this song in the style suggested in the title, we might not be playing with “beautiful sound”. This placement becomes less innocent, though, when the rest of the context is illustrated. Recall that Sound Innovations uses the term “American” more than any other book in this study and refers to Stephen Foster more than any other book in this study. In fact, Line 174, “The Blue-Tail Fly”, is explicitly labeled by the authors as an American Minstrel Tune. Perhaps a glaring oversight occurred on the part of the editors, but the implied narrative of these data all taken together is that this book is engaging deliberately in upholding white American supremacy. 

Uniformity of Content. 

Noticeable throughout all of the books in this study was a uniformity of the content. I label and interpret this to mean pieces of music or folk tunes that are printed in at least three of the five publications. For a chart of songs meeting this criteria and which books they are published in, see Appendix B on page 98. This phenomenon is worthy of 53 

discussion through the lens of multiculturalism. A common argument against changing the content in a curriculum is that there is not enough space for new content. Rather, this finding demonstrates that so much of the content is redundant among various method books. Instead, teachers, authors, and/or publishers could replace some of this preexisting content with diverse content and informational and educational contexts. For example, after a concept is introduced there are typically a few pieces of music that apply that concept in various iterations. These spaces are opportunities for authors to include multicultural musical content that differentiates their books from the other books currently on the market. 54 Chapter 6. Implications, Limitations, and Recommendations for Further Research 

In this paper, I outlined two literature bases that establish a long history of advocacy for a multicultural music education curriculum and how this curriculum has previously been analyzed, interpreted, and interrogated. The beginning band method book often defines the curriculum of the beginning band classroom and has therefore been studied many times. Previous analyses focused primarily on the pedagogical content (e.g., Byo, 1988; Robinson, 1980; Tullberg, 1992) and philosophical values (e.g., Heavner, 1995; Morris, 2000; Paschall, 2006) of each text, but have only recently scrutinized how culture is represented throughout the pages (Brittin & Sheldon, 2004; Raponi, 2015). This reflects the growing frequency and intensity with which the music education profession is calling for meaningful change to our practices, pedagogies, and content to become more culturally responsive and inclusive (Abril, 2006; Bond, 2017; Hess, 2017). The previous studies on cultural representation in beginning band method books, however, simply quantified which cultures were labeled throughout the books and the frequency with which they were presented. This present study similarly quantified which cultures were labeled and the frequency of each label, but also analyzed the contextual information regarding culture that is present in the student and teacher editions of these books. These findings were reported through four emergent themes: 55 

philosophical positioning, labels of national identity or ethnicity, content without context, and context without critical thinking. I followed the findings with discussions reflective of living and teaching music in the United States in 2021. So now, the questions must be asked: why does this matter? Why is this so important right now, in the United States, in 2021? Can we do different? Can we do better? Can we do different, better? I address these questions in this chapter. Recommendations for the profession and ideas for future research are shared as well. 

Why does this matter? 

Elliott (1995) reminds us that music is a diverse “artistic, social, and cultural” practice (p. 198). A quality music education, therefore, is one that thoroughly integrates varying ideologies, cultural backgrounds, and histories together in an aesthetically and socially meaningful way. Diversity is acknowledged, appreciated, and sustained by listening to, learning about, performing, responding to, and creating diverse musical content and contexts. If a democratic aim of education is to produce a balanced and equitable society (Dewey, 1923), then this multicultural integration is necessary. As our democracy becomes more diverse, students must be aware of and produce knowledge and skills that reflect this value. Music education, as a cultural and humanistic education, is therefore one that invites students to critique and ask questions about our cultural histories to create balanced and equitable cultural futures. But our school band programs do not reflect the cultural, racial, and socioeconomic demographics of our schools. As Elpus and Abril (2019) point out, white 56 

students and students from high socioeconomic backgrounds are dramatically overrepresented in the enrollment data. Black students, Hispanic students, and students living in poverty are as equally underrepresented in the enrollment data. Thorough integration of diverse cultures is certainly made more challenging in a band program that may appeal more to richer and whiter students. Music educators concerned with this figure examine financial barriers of instrumental music programs as a possible culprit. We know that schools with a higher population of traditionally minoritized communities do not receive as equitable funding as their whiter counterparts (Education Trust, 2005; Ladson-Billings, 2006) and this is true for band programs as well (Costa-Giomi & Chappell, 2007). Teachers must raise funds and cut additional fees to attract students who traditionally have not participated in school band programs because of financial barriers to ensure an equitable school music experience. However, lack of diversity in curriculum is another barrier that pushes students not to participate in or simply elect out of participation in various activities (e.g., San Pedro, 2018). We know that academic achievement is a predictor for minoritized students’ decisions to enroll and continue in music programs (Kinney, 2010, 2019) and that academic achievement is significantly improved when the students participate in a curriculum that is responsive to and sustaining of their cultures (Ladson-Billings, 1995; Paris, 2012). The traditionally Eurocentric curriculum of beginning band classes (Raponi, 2015) marginalizes students of color and therefore inverts the ideals of an education in a democracy (Dewey, 1923). The music education profession collectively has pushed for 57 

more diverse content and pedagogies for almost a century. Various historical rationales for this philosophy include helping students to learn to live together to combat stereotypes (Anderson, 1991), enhancing students’ regards of others so they may interact more effectively (Arnistine, 2000), and connecting students “with the personhood of other musicers and audiences in other times and places” (Elliott, 1995, p. 209). More contemporary justifications for a multicultural music education relate to the point outlined in this brief section: the central concern of music education is transmitting musical traditions from one generation to the next (Jorgensen, 2015), musical values can foster “the types of social democratic behaviors desirable for broader public participation and engagement” (Westheimer, 2015, p. 108), and a culturally diverse curriculum embraces the needs and interests of students from “diverse racial, ethnic, social class, and cultural communities.” (Campbell, 2015, p. 273). Ultimately, as Hess (2017) states: “when we engage students’ own music interests and experiences in the classroom, we communicate powerfully to students that their perspectives (and their musics) are valued and valuable” (p. 73). This justification assumes the opposite to be true as well: when we do not engage more culturally diverse musical content, we are implying these are not valuable musics or peoples worthy of formal study in a school setting. This present analysis matters because it allows the profession to reckon first with what is so that we can, if desired, imagine and act on what could be. This does not need to result in a radical shift or even a pause of instrumental music; rather, it is a valuable opportunity for needed critical self-reflection on our pedagogies, content, and the overt and covert narratives communicated to our students through our curriculum. This 58 

research establishes a baseline from which other interpretations, recommendations, and inquiries may flow. If beginning band teachers are interested in opening the curriculum so that diverse musical content and the stories told about that content are more meaningful and impactful, then a logical place to make adjustments is the beginning band method book. 

Why is this important right now – in 2021? 

NAEP data from 2019 shows that the “achievement gap” between white students and students of color is the largest it has ever been (The Nation’s Report Card, 2019). Inequality in society in the United States is growing and our education system has not been successful at disrupting this pattern (Ladson-Billings, 2006). Franklenberg, Lee, and Orfield (2003) reported that America’s public schools were more than a decade into a process of resegregation. Nearly three-fourths of Black and Latinx students attend schools that are predominantly students of color. This trend has continued into the present-day; as neighborhoods become slightly less segregated, school choice has allowed the pattern of resegregation in public schools to continue and even expand in many places (Owens, 2020; Wells, Keener, Cabral, & Cordova-Cobo, 2919). 

As mentioned before, our music programs do not, overall, reflect the demographics of students who attend schools in the United States (Elpus & Abril, 2019). Advocacies for more culturally responsive pedagogies that engage students in analyzing information through the lens of the worlds they interpret and experience continue to grow. These pedagogies – culturally relevant pedagogy (Abril, 2013; Bond, 2017; Lind & 59 

McKoy, 2016) and social justice pedagogies (Gaztambide-Fernández & Rose, 2015; Jorgensen, 2015) - encourage teachers to go beyond musical content and include contextual information that shares stories, makes connections, engages students of all backgrounds, centers diverse epistemologies, and challenges the status quo. They ask us to not just include content and context but create environments where truly critical thinking (Shaw, 2014) is the norm and stereotypes are challenged. These approaches have well-documented success in raising the academic achievement of students of color in the general education literature (Cummins, 1986; Ladson-Billings, 1995; Ladson-Billings, 2006). Curriculum in 2021 is an ethical decision; what information and whose stories should get transmitted to the next generation? Whose interpretations and experiences should be valued? Should schools serve as sites for social reproduction (Gutmann, 1999) or as sites for envisioning a more equitable society for all? If the purpose of our schools is to build a balanced society (Dewey, 1923), then in every class the content we teach, stories we tell, and questions we ask must be diverse and inclusive. Perhaps then our education system will begin paying down historical education debts (Ladson-Billings, 2006) and assist in rebuilding a more equitable society for all residents in the United States. 

What can teachers of beginning band do? 

The importance of teacher autonomy in determining which method book to use in their beginning band curriculum cannot be overstated. Since music is a subject that is not 60 

standardized and does not have high-stakes assessments tied to it, teachers of beginning band are most often the sole decision-makers when determining what to teach in their classrooms. There are many different method books available for purchase and the findings from this research outline what multicultural content and context is contained within five of the most popular texts. Teachers need to weigh their philosophical values when choosing a method book; how important is multicultural content to them, their students, and their communities? This value is also in conversation with how each text presents and reinforces various musical concepts (Byo, 1988; Tullberg, 1992), has additional online resources for students to explore (McDannald, 2012), and connects to national standards (Watkins, 2011). Ultimately, teachers must select the method book that balances these values the best for their students and communities. Findings reported here show that beginning band method books include varying degrees of multicultural content and varying depths of information about the music and people. Regardless of the book that they choose, teachers who are diligently working towards a more diverse and inclusive curriculum can highlight specifically how the provenance of a folk song is labeled in each book and determine if the context in the student and teacher books are sufficient. If they decide to supplement the information, then there are a few simple ways that they can seek out additional context. A tenet of culturally responsive (Ladson-Billings, 1995; Lind & McKoy, 2016) and culturally sustaining (Paris, 2012) pedagogies are honoring and including student expertise and epistemologies in the classroom. This means that beginning band teachers can lean on students who may have experience outside of the schools with various styles 61 

and genres of music to share both pedagogical information about music performance and about how music functions in a given group of people. Further, cross-curricular connections are advocated by the national standards for music (Shuler, Norgaard, & Blakeslee, 2014). Teachers of beginning band can involve the social studies teachers on campus to develop curriculum that enhances and builds on prior knowledge. For example, if students in band are learning the African-American spiritual, “Michael Row Your Boat Ashore”, then the information shared in band can echo and build on information taught in social studies about the role and function of religion and music in communities of previously enslaved peoples. Finally, we can use the scope and sequence charts to our advantage to analyze what musical concepts or skills are taught or reinforced on a specific line of music regardless of cultural representation. If the beginning band teacher has decided to include more diverse content in their class, they can quickly arrange or rote-teach a folk song that teaches or reinforces the same musical concepts or skills as a preexisting line of music in the book. For example, I previously taught two students in beginning band who had recently emigrated to the United States from Guyana. A popular Guyanese folk song, Kuma-Kuma Fish, uses eighth notes and the syncopated rhythm of one eighth note followed by one quarter note followed by one eighth note. The range of the melody is a perfect fourth. Instead of using the contrived line in the book that taught and reinforced this rhythm, I quickly wrote out the melody Kuma-Kuma Fish and displayed it on the projector for the class to learn. The Guyanese students – who I knew from previous interactions were excited and enthusiastic to share their culture and experience it in a school setting – were engaged and volunteered to 62 

teach the band a rhythmic accompaniment that could be performed alongside the folk song. It is important to remember, though, that when we teach Eurocentric music without context and styles of music from outside of Europe with context, we can be deploying a hidden curriculum (Vallance, 1980) that assumes and normalizes Eurocentric ideals as universal. The absence of additional context creates an assumption that prior knowledge should already include information about a given culture. The content in our beginning band method books that is representative of a certain culture should be taught with additional context – including the music that derives from European techniques or peoples. This helps de-normalize whiteness, centers diverse experiences and knowledges, and helps students experience music more fully (Bradley, 2012). 

Recommendations for Music Teacher Educators 

Considering the increased demand from teachers and researchers to include culturally diverse content in the school music classroom, music teacher educators may need to reexamine how their preservice music educators experience these conversations throughout their degree programs. As Gay (2005) notes, teacher preparation programs are “typically designed to prepare middle-class, European American candidates to teach middle-class, European American students in mainstream schools” (p. 222). Since the school music programs in the United States are even whiter and richer than the typical school demographics (Elpus & Abril, 2019), it is possible that the music education teacher candidates are even more disproportionately white than the general education 63 

teacher candidates that Gay (2005) mentioned. Conversations and open discussions about cultural diversity and inclusion need to happen with these students. These discussions should happen regularly throughout the curriculum and not be sidelined or Othered (Gay, 2005). Music teacher educators need to model the selection of culturally diverse content and responsive pedagogies in their own practices so that preservice music teachers experience it firsthand rather than simply read and talk about these pedagogies in theory. These preservice music educators should also have the practice of teaching in a culturally-responsive way as a normalized technique prior to entering the classroom. The points I make above are problematized, though, by the audition and selection procedures that determine if a student is eligible to become a music major in the first place. Koza (2008) makes the claim that a successful audition into a music degree program requires previous access to privilege. Royston and Springer (2017) report that applied private lessons faculty often make the final decisions whether or not to admit a study into a music major. Often, these professors prioritize high school grade point averages, present performance abilities, or subjective traits like teachability. While these concerns are well outside the scope of this paper, the implications of how music teacher educators can take the findings from this paper into their music education programs are indeed complicated by the demography of music education programs. 

Can we do different, better? 

Teachers of beginning band both define their curriculum using the method book and are constrained by what content and contexts are present in the method book. 64 

Advocacy for the inclusion of diverse content in this curriculum has occurred for over one century and has been carried out by leaders of the music education profession at the national level and in-service teachers. Rationales have shifted from creating a unified nation in the middle of the twentieth century, to helping peoples of various backgrounds get along with each other in the late twentieth century, to the contemporary justifications that focus on sustaining cultural identity and working to end the replication of social injustices. Findings from this study show that five popular and easily accessible beginning band method books do include a variety of diverse content, but the most frequent provenance of folk songs are the United States and western Europe. The authors of the texts do not frequently include context that promotes critical thinking. We – researchers and in-service teachers – should continue to interrogate why authors of method books are using outdated justifications for the inclusion of multicultural music. A short-term result of these inquiries may lead to teachers purchasing method books that are more aligned with their multicultural philosophies. In the long-term, publishers may gauge a shift in the demand for their books due to the presence of or lack of cultural content and they may invite their authors and editors to write an update that includes more of this material. It must be acknowledged that publishers’ decisions are constrained by basic economics. They create more of what sells and earns a profit. Editing and overhauling entire method books are monumental tasks that require significant time, energy, and finances. I do not intend to paint a negative image of book authors, editors, and publishers in this study or misrepresent their intentions. However, as discussed in 65 

Emergent Theme I, we do not know of their intentions or rationales for included multicultural musical content because they do not include this information in the book. Ultimately, the job of the authors and publishers is to make a product that is palatable for an incredibly diverse audience. This includes teachers and students in predominantly white spaces and in traditionally minoritized spaces. This audience includes teachers and students who want to avoid politics and those who consider teaching an overtly political act. It includes schools where band enrollment is smaller than ten students and schools where band enrollment is larger than 400 students. However, because method books are so popular and have such a wide reach, they also have a lot of influence. Teachers typically supplement the method books with additional information, but if culturally diverse content was to be easily accessible within the method book this would make teaching easier for the rapidly growing population of music educators who want to be more culturally responsive in their curricula. Teachers of beginning band who supplement their curriculum with diverse content can share best practices, present clinics, and write articles in journals popular amongst in-service teachers to continue to advocate for more robust change. It is noteworthy that much celebrated curriculum reform has happened in the music textbooks used in the elementary schools (Campbell, 2002) but not so much in the beginning band method books. This creates a disconnect in what musical experiences and worlds students participate in in elementary school to what they experience in middle school. Middle school teachers – specifically those who teach beginning band – can demonstrate to their colleagues that curricular revision is possible and that their students and programs are 66 

better for it. If these beginning band teachers want to move their curricula in this direction but are unsure, they can continue to pressure state organizations to host professional development clinics on these topics. Like-minded teachers of beginning band might similarly establish their own groups on social media platforms to share ideas, struggles, and successes. Perhaps a reasonable first step can be to involve the publishers’ voices in research like this. There was a lot of information open to interpretation throughout this study because the terms and philosophies printed throughout the texts were not clearly defined by the authors. Curious researchers and teachers might ask publishers, editors, and authors why they include multicultural content. This would help trace how this now-clearly stated value system impacts the content and context present or absent in the book(s). A replicated analysis with this information might yield some additional interesting findings and spark new discussions. It might also open a policy window where teachers and publishers can work together to create a curriculum that is more inclusive, tells more complete stories, and asks more critical questions. 

Limitations and Recommendations for Further Research 

The role of the teacher is critical in determining if these multicultural contents and contexts get shared and how the students engage with them. Therefore, the teacher and their philosophical values is a limitation in this study. Music inhabits a gray area in education policy: it is a mandated subject of study in the elementary level and is an elected activity in secondary schools in many states. Recent publications state that 94% 67 

of elementary schools (Parsad & Spiegelman, 2012) and 74% of high schools in the United States (Elpus, 2020) offer music instruction. Other investigations specifically on charter schools report significantly lower availability of music programs (Hedgecoth, 2017, 2020). Some states require a credit of fine arts for graduation from high school but implementations of this mandate vary widely (Arts Education Partnership, 2019). While many music subject assessments were developed in the last decade, no high-stakes consequences are attached to student performance on these tests. Put another way, a student who participates in a music class but fails any test attached to that course does not have to repeat a grade. There are national and state standards for instrumental music, but band specifically is not a standardized subject with a uniform curriculum. A large degree of curricular autonomy is afforded to the teacher who ultimately decides what to teach. Once the teacher decides what music they will use to define their curriculum (Reynolds, 2000), they then have the freedom to choose what information about each piece of music to transmit to students. Method books that include a significant amount of context in the teacher’s edition place the responsibility of sharing cultural information on the teacher. Method books that include limited cultural contexts in the student books rely on the student being curious to search for more information. For this, we must consider and interpret the findings of this research in a setting where the teacher decides whether the cultural information is shared, expanded upon, or ignored. An imaginary method book that includes diverse musical content and inclusive, thorough contexts can only be brought to life through the decisions and actions made by the teacher in the band room. 68 

A critical assumption that beginning band teachers value culturally diverse content was made in forming the need for this study. This assumption also functions as a limitation to this study. A crucial question must be asked of currently practicing teachers of beginning band in future research: does cultural representation matter when selecting a method book? Does it matter to students? If not, should it? Further, we know empirically that teachers may state a set of values but that occasionally teachers struggle to employ pedagogies and select content reflective of these philosophies. Interviews with and observations of various beginning band teachers could determine how the cultural content and context of method books is being used in the classroom, how this information is valued by teachers, and what suggestions they have to make method books more diverse. This research establishes an academic baseline of what cultural content and contexts are present in five popular and easily accessible beginning band method books using basic quantitative and qualitative methodologies. Future research can include more detailed examinations of how cultures are defined discursively throughout the texts – especially the most frequently used labels such as “American” and “Traditional”. A musicological analysis could study the history and function of each folk song in its original form to understand more about how the content of the method books creates various narratives that are taught explicitly or learned implicitly. It would be interesting to examine various method books historically to uncover when – and perhaps why – specific tunes became this common in beginning band method books. 69 Conclusion 

A limitation to this study acknowledged the role of the teacher in conjunction with the gray area of education policy that music inhabits. I view this another and more optimistic way, too; if music is not a standardized subject and teachers control the curriculum, then what limits us? What is preventing teachers from creating a more culturally responsive curriculum that is unique to their communities? Let us empower each other to think critically about the children we teach and what should be taught in a public and democratic education system. We must not be burdened and constrained by the centuries-old tradition of a utilitarian view of music education and band (Allsup & Benedict, 2008); one that historically emphasized discipline and order (Jorgensen, 1994) and Eurocentrism (McCarthy, 2015). After all, evolutions in justifications for why school music matters have occurred many times. The words of Langer, Reimer, Gardner, and Elliott all pushed the collective profession to consider how music functions in society and asked us to envision a new future: one that was more artistic, aesthetic, intelligent, and praxial. Teachers of beginning band play a crucial role in the new direction of music education as the initial instrumental instruction in a student’s life. Findings from this study, though, illustrate that beginning band method books indeed do constrain teachers from easily developing a curriculum that is more diverse and thoroughly inclusive. This research analyzed five popular and easily accessible beginning band method books to answer research questions about how culture is represented and what cultural contexts are presented throughout the pages of the student and teacher’s editions. It was determined and reported through four emergent themes that: the books in 70 

this study explicitly and implicitly positioned themselves as supportive of a multicultural music education but did not include rationales and justifications for those choices; to denote cultural information, books use a system of labels that identify provenance or national origin of a given folk song or composer; much of this multicultural content lacks additional context or information; and when there is context in the student and teacher books, it is most often trivial information about geography, climate, and language that does not include critical learning or thinking about the culture or the role of music in that culture. These findings were discussed through the contemporary lens of society in the United States in 2021. Residents of the United States are experiencing dual pandemics: one is a prolonged public health crisis and the other is the impact of long-existing systemic inequities and racism on BIPOC. Schools are reproducing these inequalities rather than disrupting them. Scholars note that standardized curricula have only widened the achievement gap between learners of various demographics (Sleeter, 2012). Teachers must reform curricula to create more thorough integration of diverse cultures. Our methodologies must be more culturally responsive – for if they are not, this, too, is another barrier constructed to equal access. This all starts with more diverse and inclusive content. As the music education profession reckons with the roles we play in excluding certain groups of students from our classes, debate has grown over the apolitical methods advocated by some and the social justice pedagogies advocated by others. Those in favor of a more culturally diverse and responsive curriculum point out that having a neutral 71 

political stance regarding this topic is actually a stance in favor of the status quo. Recommendations for further research presented in this paper proposed including a diverse sample of practicing beginning band teachers’ voices in these debates and how their thoughts intersect with the curriculum present in beginning band method books. Music must be a leader not just in desegregating our schools once again but also in thoroughly integrating our students, cultures, and communities. I think this is possible. I think this is possible in general music classes and I think this is possible in large ensemble classes like beginning band. Beginning band method books are an important tool in this work. 1A Critical Analysis of Cultural Representation in Select Beginning Band Method Books Thesis Presented in Partial Fulfillment of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Arts in the Graduate School of The Ohio State University By Daniel Taylor, BME Graduate Program in Music The Ohio State University 2021 Thesis Committee Dr. David Hedgecoth, Advisor Dr. Daryl Kinney Dr. Ann Allen 2Copyrighted by Daniel Taylor 2021 ii Abstract Using a content analysis methodology, beginning band method books were analyzed for the way authors include, identify, and provide additional context for cultural information related to the music and composers appearing in each method. An open coding process revealed the following four emergent themes: (a) authors position each book as supportive of a multicultural music education but do not include clear justifications for these values; (b) each book contains provenance labels to identify national origin or ethnicity of a melody or composer; (c) culturally diverse musical content is common but additional contexts are limited; and (d) when information is included it typically focuses on geography and language while lacking critical contexts. Findings are discussed through a contemporary lens of teaching music in the United States in 2021. Leaders of national music education organizations and their related publications began to advocate for the inclusion of multicultural music in the school music curriculum over one hundred years ago. Advocates voiced their perspectives through articles and special issues of the Music Supervisors’ Journal and Music Educators’ Journal . They also presented at conferences and organized multicultural music symposia hosted by the Music Supervisors’ National Conference (later named Music Educators’ National Conference and the National Association for Music Education). Through these advocacy strategies, national proponents of multicultural music education have consistently shared philosophical opinions, empirical research, and practical approaches to advise practicing school music educators the importance of, the effects of, and the methods of incorporating multicultural music into the content and contexts of their classrooms. Despite these sustained efforts, a lack of appreciation for cultural diversity has been a historic issue in school music education in the United States (Brittin & Sheldon, 2004; Mark, 1998). Calls to include diverse musical practices in the school music curriculum have become more urgent in recent years (e.g., Hess, 2017) as Americans become more critically aware of the inequities in society related to class, race, and culture. Bond (2017) notes that various critiques of a monocultural music curriculum have developed in the 2

last decade as scholars “reevaluate traditional structures, problematize issues of exclusion and inclusion, expand beyond Eurocentric views and teaching strategies that prioritize one way of musical knowing, and consider issues of social justice” (p. 154). These critiques have led to the creation and proliferation of pedagogies for cultural relevancy, equity, and social justice by various scholars in music education (Jorgensen, 2015; Lind & McKoy, 2016). The inclusion of multicultural music in the curriculum is a foundational component of these philosophies (Campbell, 2015). In a music classroom, the repertoire and other musical content selected for study “creates the framework… for a music curriculum that fosters the musical growth of our students” (Reynolds, 2000, p. 31). The curriculum in beginning band classrooms across the United States typically centers the use of a method book (Raponi, 2015). These books are used to develop technique and learn musical concepts in a logically sequenced manner as prescribed by the authors. Curriculum is a “body of knowledge that is taught in schools and supported by texts in the wider society” (Au, Brown, & Calderón, 2016, p. 120). Beginning band method books center the curriculum and determine what information students will learn; therefore, they meet the standard to be called the textbook of the music class (Altbach, 1991). The field of music education is lacking critical analysis of how various cultural groups are represented in the common teaching materials used to form the school music curriculum across all grade levels (Schmidt, 1999). Previous analyses have celebrated the progress made in the elementary school curriculum (Campbell, 2002), but little critical thinking about cultural representation in secondary school curricular materials, 3

particularly beginning band method books, has occurred. The scholarship that has been published on beginning band method books has quantified cultural representation as a percentage of content and neglected the qualitative analysis of the cultural contexts that are present in each book (Brittin & Sheldon, 2004; Raponi, 2015). As Bradley (2012) states, “without knowledge of context, full meaning [of music] cannot truly be experienced” (p. 189). This thesis continues the tradition of quantifying cultural representation throughout selected beginning band method books. I also examine the student and teacher editions of each book for what contextual information about culture is present. This information is grouped into emergent themes applicable across data sets representative of the selected beginning band method books and interpreted, problematized, and discussed through a contemporary lens of teaching music in the United States today. 

Author Positionality 

I acknowledge my positionality in forming these discussions in response to data. I write this thesis as a half-white, half-Cuban, cisgendered gay male who only saw the more normalized or safest aspects of his identity – the white and cisgendered male facets – represented or discussed in curriculum in the United States while growing up. I write this thesis as a person who taught using beginning band method books for nine years and tried to make my curriculum more culturally responsive so that my students could see themselves, engage with music of various cultures, and learn about cultural contributions, points of contact between cultures, and have a more complete experience 4

of music. I write this thesis as a person who believes that what constitutes public school music curriculum is a political choice, an aesthetic choice, and – most importantly – an ethical choice. A culturally diverse democracy demands that our schools acknowledge, celebrate, and sustain our differences rather than vilify and homogenize them. To me, a quality music education is one that more thoroughly integrates varying ideologies, cultural backgrounds, and histories together. Music can make humans aware of and empathetic towards other humans’ humanness. Listening to, learning about, performing, responding to, and creating music allows children from a young age to identify as a member of a community. Music study applies to all humans, connects us to our past, and can allow for democratic engagement by all citizens. If a democratic aim of education is to produce a balanced and equitable society (Dewey, 1923), then multicultural integration is necessary. As our democracy becomes more diverse, students must be aware of and produce knowledge and skills that reflect this value. A purpose of this paper is to interpret data qualitatively and remark on it through the lens of living in the United States in 2021. Residents in the United States are experiencing dual pandemics: a coronavirus and the effects of systemic racism and intolerance. Hate crimes have spiked, the one-year anniversary of the murder of Breonna Taylor passed the week prior to writing this chapter, the trial for the murderer of George Floyd began two weeks prior to writing this chapter, and the day that I sat down to write these words was March 17, 2021 – the day that Asian women were targeted and murdered by a white supremacist in Atlanta, GA. The capitol of the United States was attacked three months ago by a group of white supremacists attempting a coup by 5

violently demanding lawmakers invalidate the votes of metropolitan areas inhabited by Black voters. Violence and structural inequalities based on cultural difference are prevalent in American society today. Prior to graduate school, I taught middle school band and general music for nine years. As a music teacher, I believe that culturally diverse democracies - such as that of the United States - must have a public-school music curriculum that aids in disrupting the societal inequities and cultural hierarchies that lead to misunderstanding, inequity of opportunity, and even violence. This curriculum must be inclusive and pluralistic to create thorough integration, remove racial biases, and end the historic practice of education-as-assimilation. This thorough integration is a matter of distributive justice (Gutmann, 1999). All students must have equitable access to education. Curricula must not assimilate students into a reified social hierarchy or reinvent racial prejudices in the American public. Rather, curricula must reflect the cultural diversity and plurality of the country so that students can challenge assumptions and engage critically with diverse content that fosters dialogue regarding cultural contributions and structural inequities. In my years as a practicing music teacher, though, I discovered that the materials I imagined including in a curriculum that supported this vision were not easily accessible. In this thesis, I seek to quantify the multicultural content and qualitatively analyze the multicultural contexts of various beginning band method books. What once was anecdotal evidence of my experiences has developed into an empirical analysis to discover important truths about who and what is included or excluded in the curricular foundations we have easy access to as beginning band teachers. 6

No specific framework or theory was selected to guide the analysis in this thesis because the inclusion of culturally diverse curricular content is a tenet of many: culturally-relevant pedagogy (Ladson-Billings, 1995; Lind & McKoy, 2016), culturally-sustaining pedagogy (Paris, 2012), and social justice pedagogy (e.g., Gaztambide-Fernández & Rose, 2015). Decisions were made about how to define data and then themes inevitably formed through data analysis, but the following discussions are ultimately partially informed by my experiences, philosophies, and values. The research questions that guide this inquiry are: 1. How is cultural diversity represented in selected beginning band method books? 2. When culturally diverse material is presented, what contextual information about these cultures is included in these texts? Chapter 2 presents a review of extant literature to trace the history of multicultural music advocacy in the United States and what previous method book content analyses have discovered. Methodological details of data collection and analysis are shared in Chapter 3, followed by a presentation of findings from the content analysis itself in Chapter 4. Chapter 5 provides a discussion in response to the findings of the content analysis, and Chapter 6 shares implications and limitations of this study to conclude the thesis. 7Chapter 2. Review of Literature The Development of a Culturally Diverse Music Curriculum 

Professional music educators have been advocating for the creation of a culturally diverse school music curriculum for decades. Scholars who advocate for cultural diversity in music education have focused on “knowing and validating students’ cultural heritage(s), developing a disposition to affirm students’ cultural capital, and incorporating multicultural materials” (Bond, 2017, p. 168). To borrow terminology from Sleeter and Grant (1987), some music educators have published approaches to multicultural education that can be categorized as “human relations” (p. 422). Scholars advocate for the inclusion of diverse materials because they purport to help students learn to live together to combat stereotypes (Anderson, 1991), enhance students’ regard of others so they may interact more effectively (Arnistine, 2000), and “connect [students] with the personhood of other musicers and audiences in other times and places” (Elliott, 1995, p. 209). Other music educators, however, have pushed for the broadening of the school music curriculum based on different arguments. For example, an approach for multicultural curricula is described by Anderson (1983) when he writes “in considering the teacher as a translator of culture, it seems particularly appropriate that music programs in the United States should reflect…the great ethnic heritage of the American 8

people” (p. 32). The materials used in these music programs should be placed alongside “students’ own musics, experiences, and interests” (Hess, 2017, p. 72). Still others advocate a single group studies approach (Sleeter & Grant, 1987) that seeks to “broaden and enrich the background that students acquire from the environment in which they are growing up” (Arnistine, 2000, p. 5) and reveal a deeper understanding of multicultural influences on popular forms of music (Dodds, 1983). Dunbar-Hall (2005) promotes a social reconstructionist view (Sleeter & Grant, 1987) by labeling music education as “cultural studies: a subject concerned with uncovering the differences and power relationships among groups of people and their cultures” (pp. 33-34). Regardless of the theoretical grounding and rationales used, the frequency and urgency with which culturally diverse school music is advocated has rapidly increased in recent years. Music Educators’ Journal published 21 articles between 2000-2010 that were related to multiculturalism, diversity, and equity. Forty-six articles on the same topics were published between 2010-2020. Music Educators’ Journal now features an occasional spotlight on equity and social justice as the profession demonstrates a “firm commitment to serve the diverse student populations of the United States and the world” (Hess, 2017, p. 71). Patterns exist among the rationales used to promote musical diversity in the schools throughout the development of music education in America. These trends are often reflected in the greater American sociopolitical climate (Kang, 2016; Mark, 1999). It is appropriate to analyze the political and social norms that impacted music education alongside the published discourse found in the pages of the Music Educators’ Journal 9

because the publication has “always served as the primary communication vehicle for [the music education] profession, and it has always included announcements and news items relevant to the times…” (Freer, 2013, p. 57). Themed conferences and symposia sponsored by the National Association for Music Education – previously the Music Supervisors’ National Conference and the Music Educators’ National Conference – also help to illustrate how advocacy for a multicultural music education developed. A brief overview of American society and the discourse surrounding a multicultural music education provides important context which helps the reader better understand the magnitude of the philosophical shifts in music education over time. In the next section, I outline key points in the development of the philosophy for a culturally diverse music education. 

1960 – 1967: The Social Imperative for Multiculturalism 

The decade between 1960 and 1970 was pivotal in building momentum for the growing movement within music education advocating for the inclusion of multicultural musics in the school music education curriculum. Campbell (2002) writes: The civil rights movement of the 1960s was the more immediate impetus for the formulation of multicultural education in the US because this was a time when ethnic minority groups initiated actions to make others aware of the perspectives and needs of their underrecognized groups (p. 28). Social upheaval and a shifting of cultural values were occurring in the American public (Kidd, 1984). The Civil Rights movement brought recognition to disenfranchised people. 10 

Recognition of social inequalities between people of various races, uneven access to democratic participation, and negative effects of long-term white hegemony in the United States was thrust into the public debate. The music education profession responded tepidly at first and then later in profound ways during this decade. An example of a hesitant reaction to advocacy for a more diverse school music curriculum is illustrated in the professional response to the 1963 Yale Seminar on Music Education. This gathering of ethnomusicologists examined materials used in American school music programs. Seminar attendees examined materials used in American school music programs, were highly critical of the school music curriculum, and interrogated the penchant of music educators to focus on superficial musical experiences instead of the aesthetic impact of music study (Mark & Gary, 2007). The leaders of the Yale seminar believed that the repertoire used in school music programs was too restricted to Western music. They recommended expanding the curriculum to include jazz and folk music from many different cultures. The final report read: ...many ethnic groups possess highly sophisticated musical cultures... any program of music instruction in the schools that does not find a place for... these cultures and their music is turning its back on one of the most compelling realities of our time (Palisca, 1964, p. 3). The Yale Seminar did not have an immediate impact on the daily lives of music educators in America because educators were not involved in the discussions, conference, or crafting of the final resolution. Hoffer (1979) outlines that music educators believed the ethnomusicologists who led the Yale Seminar had both a limited understanding of 11 

and a biased lens through which they viewed the education profession. The resolution from the end of the seminar was criticized as being unfairly critical of the Eurocentrism of the school music curriculum. The Yale Seminar did, however, lead to future events that pushed the profession to change (Mark & Gary, 2007). An increasing number of MENC conferences in the 1960s included student performances featuring diverse and innovative multicultural music (Anderson, 1974). McCarthy (1997) reports that the 1966 national MENC conference at Interlochen, Michigan – three years after the Yale Seminar – revealed a shift away from placid remarks on the power of music to the importance of uniting through learning other cultures’ music. Guidelines were established to institute a multicultural philosophy of music education into school music programs. The following year, the Music Educators’ Journal published a speech from the conference that challenged American music programs to include methods and materials from other cultures (Kraus, 1967). 

1967 – 1969: The Tanglewood Symposium and the GO Project 

The Tanglewood Symposium of 1967 represents the most significant step forward for the multicultural perspective in music education (Anderson, 1992). This meeting of leading music educators, administrators, and ethnomusicologists was a self-study of the music education profession led by MENC (Mark & Gary, 2007). Volk (1993) argues that the final declaration of the Tanglewood Symposium has “become the landmark document in multicultural music education, which recognizes the importance of all musics within 12 

the school curriculum” (p. 228). The declaration states, in no uncertain terms, the awareness of the need to expand the repertoire (Kidd, 1984) in saying “Music for all periods, styles, forms, and cultures belong in the curriculum” (Choate, 1968, p. 139). The Goals and Objectives Project of 1968 began to implement the recommendations of the Tanglewood Symposium. The leaders of the project identified immediate needs to be addressed. Important for the multicultural music education movement was the fourth need: “advance the teaching of music of all periods, styles, forms, and cultures” (Mark & Gary, 2007, pp. 365-366). 

1970 – 1980: Implementation of the charges of the Tanglewood Declaration 

MENC was tasked with the implementation of the recommendations from the Tanglewood Symposium. The years between 1970 and 1980 were critical in determining if the ideas from Tanglewood would be adopted and implemented by classroom music teachers. MENC formally declared that worldwide conformity in musical taste and music education is dangerous to cultural variety during this time (McCarthy, 1997). Every MENC conference of this decade was focused on multicultural music education. Elementary music teachers were often the target audience of these performances and lectures (Volk, 1993). The 1970 conference included the Ethnic Musics Institute. African drumming ensembles performed, discussions on issues in a Westernized music education were held, and steel pan ensembles were introduced at the national level for the very first time. 13 

Important committees inside of MENC also developed during this time period. The Black Music Caucus was initiated in 1972 as a reaction against the reality that the sessions on multiculturalism and negro spirituals were led by white people (McCarroll, 2016). The 1974 MENC conference created the Minority Concerns Commission (Volk, 1993). They recommended that “all units of MENC...when planning programs and classroom activities must make efforts to include representative music from the various ethnic groups that comprise our nation...” (Washington, 1983, p. 67). The first special issue of the Music Educators’ Journal to address multiculturalism was published in 1972 – “Music in World Cultures” (Volk, 1993). It included curricular materials of African and African American musics for use in the classroom (Kidd, 1984). The journal was divided into three sections: an overview of world musical cultures (Mead, 1972), a section on persuading music teachers to realize the imperative for multicultural music education (Seeger, 1972; Tait, 1972), and reviews of multicultural resources (Volk, 1993). This important moment marks the first time multicultural music education was centered in the foremost publication of the profession to communicate methods and pedagogies that teachers across the United States could use in their classrooms to help diversify their curricula. 

1980 – 1990: The Multicultural Imperative 

The momentum for the creation of a multicultural music education continued to grow during this decade. In 1983, the Music Educators’ Journal published its second special focus issue on world music – “The Multicultural Imperative” (Volk, 1993). 14 

Articles urged music teachers to no longer be insular in their selection of materials (Gamble, 1983) and pointed out that most music teachers acknowledge and value the musics of various cultures but teach the music of only one culture (Garfias, 1983). Further, it acknowledged that much of the history of music education in America was separate and unequal (Heller, 1983). The journal was much more direct with teachers than the previous special issue. Many music educators were still teaching a decidedly Western curriculum despite all of the work MENC had done to increase resources and access to multicultural materials. 

1990 – 1999: Multicultural approaches to music education 

The first MENC conference of the decade was titled “Multicultural Approaches to Music Education” (McCarthy, 2007). This symposium highlighted the culture and music of African Americans, Asian Americans, Hispanic Americans, and Native Americans (Volk, 1993). Edwin Schupman, a Creek Indian, stated at the conference that “the role of the music educator has not yet been realized in terms of broadening the multicultural horizons of their students, of promoting human understanding, and tolerance for racial and cultural difference” (Anderson, 1991). The symposium concluded with the following resolutions: we will seek to ensure that multicultural approaches to teaching will be incorporated into every elementary and secondary school music curriculum. Multicultural approaches to teaching music will be incorporated into all phases of teacher education... Music teachers will seek to assist students in understanding 15 

that there are many different but equally valid forms of musical expression... Instruction will include not only the study of other musics but the relationship to their respective cultures... MENC will encourage national accrediting groups to require broad, multicultural perspectives for all education programs. (Anderson, 1991, p. 33) It is important to recognize that this was the first time MENC stated its intention to require multicultural music education in primary and secondary schools. MENC published another special issue aimed at practitioners in 1992 titled “Multicultural Music Education” (Volk, 1993). This was the third time in twenty years that MENC, through the Music Educators’ Journal , published an entire issue devoted to the philosophy and pedagogy of multicultural music education. The issue contained pedagogical techniques (Campbell, 1992), resource and recording lists (Tucker, 1992), and ideas for including multicultural music in an instrumental setting (Schmid, 1992). This third special issue on multiculturalism was meant to give teachers the specific tools needed to create a diverse curriculum. The 1995 and 1996 issues of the Music Educators’ Journal contained eight articles by ethnomusicologists answering questions from teachers regarding multicultural issues. Kang (2016) reports that the 1995 MENC conference jointly hosted by the Society for Ethnomusicology and the Smithsonian Institute was aptly named “The Multicultural Symposium”. The symposium once again reaffirmed the need for multicultural music education in the classroom. 16 2000 – present: Building on the past and envisioning the future As stated previously, the frequency of publications supporting, detailing, or advocating for a diverse music curriculum increased significantly in these two most recent decades. This section cannot serve as an exhaustive overview within the scope of this paper. However, I will conclude this portion of the review of literature by touching on some important moments and summarizing trends in the contemporary development of multicultural music education. The collection of voices advocating for diverse cultural representation in the school music curriculum continued to grow louder and larger at the beginning of the 21 st 

century. A distinguished group of music educators and researchers assembled at the Florida State University in Tallahassee, Florida to participate in the Housewright Symposium. Following the symposium, MENC published a report to summarize and detail the discussions that took place. The report concluded with a sweeping declaration which mostly reaffirmed, built on, and modernized similar sentiments shared during the Tanglewood Symposium. The fourth line of the declaration states that “all music has a place in the curriculum… music educators need to be aware of other music that people experience and be able to integrate it into classroom music instruction” (Hinckley, 2000, p. 219). During these most recent two decades, 67 articles have been published in the 

Music Educators Journal relating either tangentially or directly speaking about multicultural music education. A noticeable difference from previous decades is that these articles are more consistently spread out among issues of the journal instead of 17 being grouped into a singular special focus issue. Articles are more varied in their aims, too: some are on the musical traditions of very specific cultures and groups of people (e.g., Arya, 2015; Barry & Conlon, 2003; Bowman, 2008; Campbell & Beegle, 2003; Dekaney & Cunningham, 2009; Damm, 2015; Park, 2013; Torchon, 2018; Whitener, 2017) and others are more philosophical to detail the need for a culturally diverse music education (e.g., Abril, 2006; Campbell, 2002; Gray, 2019; Hoffman, 2013; Howard, 2020; Huisman-Koops, 2010; Kelly & VanWeelden, 2004; Peters, 2016; Salvador, 2019; Shaw, 2012; Shaw, 2014). A notable exception was a special issue in 2012 that, for the first time in the history of the Music Educators Journal , highlighted social justice issues in music education. Articles in this issue detailed a new philosophy of music education (Allsup & Shieh, 2012), socioeconomic issues and barriers (Bates, 2012; DeLorenzo, 2012), and specific suggestions for curricular reform (Hoffman, 2012; Shaw, 2012). The special issue on social justice laid the groundwork for the occasional new column on social justice (Hess, 2017) that “demonstrates a commitment to serve the diverse student populations of the United States and the world” (p. 71). It is important to note that the authors of these articles seldomly addressed these philosophies and calls to action to band specifically. This section of the review of literature outlined some important events and historical trends in the development of the advocacy for a multicultural music education. Sociopolitical events such as the Civil Rights Movement in the United States throughout the twentieth century often triggered a response from the music education profession. In the 21 st century, though, music educators and researchers alike are attempting to lead as 18 

our society becomes more collectively aware of injustices that are reproduced by the education system. The amount of published advocacy has increased and the contemporary justifications for culturally diverse material are rooted in multiple conceptions of social justice (Jorgensen, 2015). No matter what pedagogies are advocated or when the advocacy occurred, one thing has been consistent throughout the century of highlighting the need for a multicultural music education: it starts with a curriculum that centers diverse musical content. For that reason, it is wise to analyze school music curricula to determine what musical content is present. The curriculum of the beginning band room typically centers the use of a method book (Raponi, 2015); therefore, a content analyses of these books would assist in identifying multicultural content that is easily accessible to be presented in beginning band classrooms. Many studies of method books have been previously conducted. I outline their findings in the next section. 

Method Book Analyses of Musical Concepts 

The group of method book content analyses described in this section is by no means exhaustive. A brief search in the ERIC and ProQuest databases helped me identify more than thirty analyses that fit this description. However, I chose to highlight these few because they innovated the field of method book analysis and are consistently cited throughout the literature. Nelson (1959) published the first analysis of beginning band method books. He studied books published during the decade of the 1950s for the following information: appropriate grade level, technical advantages and disadvantages, ensemble development, and general appearance and format. These categories were 19 

developed using the Criteria for Evaluation of Textbooks in the Field of Music for the State of California. Each domain was scored and then the books were ranked from best to worst. While an overwhelming number of subjective decisions and researcher biases formed the definitions and overall rankings in his work, the Nelson study is notable since it is the first to challenge the profession to systematically compare beginning band method books to each other. Later scholars analyzed more specific musical concepts and the sequence in which they appear throughout beginning band method books. Robinson (1980), Byo (1988), and Tullberg (1992) all explored and documented the melodic and harmonic material including pitches, ranges, rhythms, musical terms, and the considerations and accommodations made for various instruments throughout the books. Robinson developed a survey with music teachers to rank which musical concepts were the most important and, therefore, which book fit the needs of teachers the most. Byo presented his analysis without ranking or adjudicating the materials: rather, he analyzed the tonal, rhythmic, and physical features of the book so that each teacher could choose the appropriate book based on their “clearly defined personal philosophy and preferences” (Byo, 1988, p. 21). Tullberg (1992) builds on these previous analyses and uses similar methodology to identify similarities and differences among five method books that publishers predicted would be popular. 20 Method Book Content as a Reflection of Philosophical Values 

Other beginning band method book content analyses can be categorized based on their attempts to identify represented philosophical values. This group of analyses is more diverse in scope than those who studied purely musical content. For example, scholars have worked to label principles that align with discovery learning (Groeling, 1975), the Kodály method (Buttery, 1983), Pestalozzian philosophies of teaching and learning (Morris, 2000), the national music standards (Watkins, 2011), technological resources (McDannald, 2012), and research on motor movement and auditory perception (Helton, 2014). Of relevance to the present investigation, though, are two studies that analyzed beginning band method books for principles of comprehensive musicianship (Heavner, 1995; Paschall, 2006). Comprehensive musicianship is a theoretical model for music teaching that consists of five categories: concepts, content, activities, instructional literature, and evaluation (Heavner, 1995). Heavner positioned her study in the changing landscape of education: one that was now more standards-focused and student-centered (McDannald, 2012). She developed a theoretical model of comprehensive musicianship and a survey that teachers could use to evaluate how well each selected method book aligned to each of the five categories in the model. One survey question related to the books’ variety of Western and non-Western music (Heaver, 1995, p. 46). While quantification and evaluation of multicultural content were not the focuses of her study, she reports that method books overall lacked “Eastern” and “African” music (p. 139). 21 

Paschall (2006) went a step further by comparing method books on the observable traits of comprehensive musicianship and adherence to the national arts standards. The ninth music content standard for grades 5-8, in which beginning band is most frequently taught, refers to understanding music in relation to history and culture. Paschall conflated country of origin and culture and listed which countries/cultures were represented in five different beginning band books. After combining this national standard with the inclusion of non-Western musics in the comprehensive musicianship philosophy, Paschall was able to identify the beginning band books that adhered to specific principles of comprehensive musicianship and published national standards. Her results showed that of the five books included in her analysis, only one adhered to both. However, since multiculturalism is only found tangentially in one tenet of comprehensive musicianship and one national standard, it was not the focus of either of these studies. 

Method Book Analyses of Cultural Representation 

Only two published studies explicitly analyze beginning band method books for cultural representation. Both analyses occurred within the last fifteen years and both were published in journals that have a wide audience of practicing music teachers. While completed by different researchers, the studies were conducted with similar methodologies and came to similar conclusions. The more recent study compares the results of the two to identify trends in the data. I detail both analyses below since my thesis project will join with theirs and fill a gap in the literature created by their studies. 22 

Brittin and Sheldon (2004) analyzed five beginning band method books published between 1993-2003. Each musical exercise was categorized based on the information that was provided by the publisher, i.e., composer, type of music, country of origin / culture, and whether the exercise was authentic or “contrived” – meaning if it was an exercise written specifically for a pedagogical function. Contrived music ranged from 37% - 52% of the exercises in the included books. Music originating in the United States dominated all the authentic music found in the books. French, British, and Slavic cultures were the next most represented throughout the authentic musical exercises. These findings were compared to a same analysis of the first published heterogenous band method book from 1924, The Universal Teacher , to “gain perspective and ascertain changes in the last 80 years” (Brittin & Sheldon, 2004, p. 49). This comparison showed that there has been a slight increase – 5% on average – in the amount of authentic music included in band method books originating in countries other than the United States over the previous eight decades. The authors did not say why a culturally diverse music curriculum is important. Sources referenced in their review of literature allude to the need to appreciate different cultures, broaden students’ listening preferences, and increase student engagement. Raponi (2015) employed a different methodology, analyzed different method books, and coded data differently than Brittin and Sheldon (2004). Books were selected if they were published between 2010-2012 and were easily accessible in Canada. Cultural representation was quantified as a percentage of total musical exercises in each method book and cultures were categorized as white, non-white, and Black. In her findings, 23 

Raponi draws comparisons between the two studies by fitting her methodology and data categorization onto the Brittin and Sheldon (2004) findings. She determined that the 2004 study showed 92% of the music to be representation of white cultures, 5% non-white, and 2% Black. In her own 2015 analysis, Raponi determined that 84% of the music was representative of white cultures, 9% non-white, and 6% Black. She noted that while there is a difference, there seems to still be a “much higher value placed on melodies from the Western canon and white cultures…” (Raponi, 2015, Discussion section, para. 2). Raponi approached her analysis with the lens of a currently practicing middle school band director in a densely populated and highly diverse urban core in Canada. She writes of the importance of teaching culturally diverse musics as a way of “reinforc[ing] the cultural heritage of the individual student” (Raponi, 2015, Introduction section, para. 1). While these two studies share the goal of codifying cultural representation in beginning band method books, the authors categorized data differently. Both quantified the countries of origin of various authentic musical examples in each. Raponi (2015) then classified various cultures as white, non-white, or black. Neither Brittin and Sheldon (2004) nor Raponi (2015) analyzed student-facing materials or teacher-facing materials for what contexts or stories of each various culture are presented. Further, authors of these two studies did not propose to analyze their findings with a lens of contemporary cultural issues and politics. My study aims to similarly analyze cultural representation but includes the written and illustrated contexts in student and teacher’s editions of each method book. Additionally, my study fills a gap in the literature by discussing the findings grounded in the context of teaching music in the United States in 2021. 24 Chapter 3. Research Design and Procedure 

The purpose of this study was to analyze the cultural content and contexts of beginning band method books. Specific research questions were: 1. How is cultural diversity represented in selected beginning band method books? 2. When culturally diverse material is presented, what contextual information about these cultures is included in these texts? 

Selection of Books for this Analysis 

Five beginning band method books were selected for analysis. These books were selected because they are easily accessible in the United States and are perceived to be popular because of their pervasive presence at state, regional, and national professional development conferences and use in the classroom. The books were all either originally published or revised within the 21 st century. The method books chosen for study were: 

1. Accent on Achievement (O’Reilly & Williams, 2001) 

2. Essential Elements (Lautzenheiser et al., 2004) 3. Sound Innovations (Sheldon, Boonshaft, Black, & Phillips, 2010) 4. Standard of Excellence (Pearson, 2004) 25 

5. Traditions of Excellence (Pearson & Nowlin, 2010) I contacted the publisher of each method book to request a student copy. Each publisher shipped the student copy to my personal address free of charge. The Bb Clarinet student book of each publication was used in this study to control for varying information presented in books for different instruments. I purchased the teacher’s edition of each book after requesting and being granted funds through the Music Education department at The Ohio State University. Teacher’s edition books were ordered through the local music retailer. Supplemental materials, i.e., the Teacher’s Resource Kit referred to throughout 

Accent on Achievement , were not purchased and therefore not included in this analysis. Previous studies of beginning band method books that analyzed cultural content focused primarily on the labels that each book uses to refer to provenance, national identity, and ethnicity (Brittin & Sheldon, 2004; Raponi, 2015). I also surveyed each book for a similar use of labels to ensure that they included clearly stated cultural information printed in both the student book and teacher’s edition. Since this study goes beyond the quantification of content and analyzes contexts and additional information, I expanded the definition of clearly stated cultural information to include labels that refer to national identity or ethnicity, illustrations, photographs, or any other printed information about a cultural contribution, cultural artifact, or point of contact between cultures. For example, Accent on Achievement includes illustrations in the student book that communicates cultural information. A drawing of hula dancing is placed next to “Aloha ‘Oe” and an illustration of a gondola is printed above “Carnival of Venice”. Names of composers were counted as data in this study only if the additional context 26 

located within the student or teacher book mentioned their nationality or cultural identity. Information regarding historical time periods or music theory was included as valid data only if it specifically and explicitly mentioned national identity or ethnicity. This decision was modeled after the Brittin and Sheldon (2004) study. Musical accompaniments for each exercise – written or recorded – were not included in this analysis because of the wide fluctuation in the overtly subjective analysis of authenticity. 

Data Collection Procedure 

I reviewed the student book and teacher’s edition of each publication to determine if explicit cultural information was present. Glossaries and appendices were only included if they were specifically referred to in the main content of the book. Introductory pages were included as data if there was pedagogical information that one could reasonably assume would be taught in the beginning band method book including but not limited to: posture, instrument assembly, and hand position. Music that that was printed specifically for a certain instrument was not included as it would not be consistent throughout the student book for each different instrument. Easily identifiable cultural information was first coded as data (Saldaña & Omasta, 2016) and then typed exactly as it appeared in the student book and teacher’s edition onto an Excel spreadsheet. This open coding process - sometimes called initial coding - allowed me to extract content from the texts into small units for reflection and analysis. Each of the ten books – five student and five teacher – was labeled as an individual data set. There was significantly more data collected from the teacher’s editions because of the difference in length and detail between them and the student 27 

books. The research questions guided this process as I searched for themes within each individual data set and themes common to all data sets. Data was color-coded on Excel as themes emerged. This helped to identify connections between the books which were all published by different publishers, included different music, and provided widely varying amounts of easily identifiable cultural information as data. In total, the coded data led to the discovery of four emergent themes consistent across all books analyzed in the study. I labeled the emergent themes as follows: 1. Philosophical Positioning 2. National Identity and/or Ethnicity Labels 3. Content Without Context 4. Context Without Critical Thinking Data that led to the formation of these emergent themes are included in Chapter 4. Additional subthemes applicable to an individual data set were also uncovered. These data are important and worthy of inclusion in this content analysis because of the discussions and questions that they present. To offer a more comprehensive understanding of the current investigation, I have decided to include this information following the discussion on emergent themes. These data are included in the section labeled “(dis)Honorable Mentions”. The data collected from the five publications in this study are used to answer the previously stated research questions. In the next section I present findings as they relate to my research questions. 28 Chapter 4. Findings 

The purpose of this study was to analyze the cultural content and contexts of selected beginning band method books. The books were selected purposefully for their popular use in the classroom. I analyzed both the student book and teacher’s edition for each publication, resulting in ten total individual data sets. Each book provided data regarding cultural content and contexts.
