I purchased the teacher’s edition of each book after requesting and being granted funds through the Music Education department at The Ohio State University. Teacher’s edition books were ordered through the local music retailer. Supplemental materials, i.e., the Teacher’s Resource Kit referred to throughout 

Accent on Achievement , were not purchased and therefore not included in this analysis. Previous studies of beginning band method books that analyzed cultural content focused primarily on the labels that each book uses to refer to provenance, national identity, and ethnicity (Brittin & Sheldon, 2004; Raponi, 2015). I also surveyed each book for a similar use of labels to ensure that they included clearly stated cultural information printed in both the student book and teacher’s edition. Since this study goes beyond the quantification of content and analyzes contexts and additional information, I expanded the definition of clearly stated cultural information to include labels that refer to national identity or ethnicity, illustrations, photographs, or any other printed information about a cultural contribution, cultural artifact, or point of contact between cultures. For example, Accent on Achievement includes illustrations in the student book that communicates cultural information. A drawing of hula dancing is placed next to “Aloha ‘Oe” and an illustration of a gondola is printed above “Carnival of Venice”. Names of composers were counted as data in this study only if the additional context 26 

located within the student or teacher book mentioned their nationality or cultural identity. Information regarding historical time periods or music theory was included as valid data only if it specifically and explicitly mentioned national identity or ethnicity. This decision was modeled after the Brittin and Sheldon (2004) study. Musical accompaniments for each exercise – written or recorded – were not included in this analysis because of the wide fluctuation in the overtly subjective analysis of authenticity. 

Data Collection Procedure 

I reviewed the student book and teacher’s edition of each publication to determine if explicit cultural information was present. Glossaries and appendices were only included if they were specifically referred to in the main content of the book. Introductory pages were included as data if there was pedagogical information that one could reasonably assume would be taught in the beginning band method book including but not limited to: posture, instrument assembly, and hand position. Music that that was printed specifically for a certain instrument was not included as it would not be consistent throughout the student book for each different instrument. Easily identifiable cultural information was first coded as data (Saldaña & Omasta, 2016) and then typed exactly as it appeared in the student book and teacher’s edition onto an Excel spreadsheet. This open coding process - sometimes called initial coding - allowed me to extract content from the texts into small units for reflection and analysis. Each of the ten books – five student and five teacher – was labeled as an individual data set. There was significantly more data collected from the teacher’s editions because of the difference in length and detail between them and the student 27 

books. The research questions guided this process as I searched for themes within each individual data set and themes common to all data sets. Data was color-coded on Excel as themes emerged. This helped to identify connections between the books which were all published by different publishers, included different music, and provided widely varying amounts of easily identifiable cultural information as data. In total, the coded data led to the discovery of four emergent themes consistent across all books analyzed in the study. I labeled the emergent themes as follows: 1. Philosophical Positioning 2. National Identity and/or Ethnicity Labels 3. Content Without Context 4. Context Without Critical Thinking Data that led to the formation of these emergent themes are included in Chapter 4. Additional subthemes applicable to an individual data set were also uncovered. These data are important and worthy of inclusion in this content analysis because of the discussions and questions that they present. To offer a more comprehensive understanding of the current investigation, I have decided to include this information following the discussion on emergent themes. These data are included in the section labeled “(dis)Honorable Mentions”. The data collected from the five publications in this study are used to answer the previously stated research questions. In the next section I present findings as they relate to my research questions. 28 Chapter 4. Findings 

The purpose of this study was to analyze the cultural content and contexts of selected beginning band method books. The books were selected purposefully for their popular use in the classroom. I analyzed both the student book and teacher’s edition for each publication, resulting in ten total individual data sets. Each book provided data regarding cultural content and contexts. These data were analyzed and coded to identify emergent themes that could connect findings between each of the texts. Selected additional data that was unable to be synthesized under a generalizable emergent theme but that will provoke important discussion and implications will be included in the next chapter. The themes discussed in this section are: 1. Emergent Theme I: Philosophical Positioning 2. Emergent Theme II: Identity Labels 3. Emergent Theme III: Content Without Context 4. Emergent Theme IV: Context Without Critical Thinking 

Emergent Theme I: Philosophical Positioning 

Each of the books included in this study contains introductory material that informs both the student and the teacher what the intended purposes and outcomes of 29 

study using a particular text are. These introductions also outline specific musical information to be presented to students throughout the book. As Apple (1992) points out, knowledge in textbooks is not neutral or uncontested; it defines the nature of the discipline and what is valuable and worthy of transmitting to children. The scope and sequence of material presented in a beginning band method book therefore represents a practical expression of philosophical values (Jorgensen, 2014) by the authors, and/or the publishers, and/or the public who purchase and consume their products. These philosophical positions are either stated explicitly or inductively observed by analyzing the political act of including or excluding certain content and contexts from the pages of the method books. These data are found on the first few pages of the teacher’s edition. The authors of each book use these opening sections to outline what musical content is in the book. The musical content is often presented in a chart to illustrate the sequence with which concepts are introduced. These charts often show pitches, rhythms, articulations, and other relevant vocabulary. The choice of what information to include not just on these charts but also in sum throughout the method creates implicit value statements of what information is worthy and appropriate for transmission to beginning band students. The scope and sequence charts in Standard of Excellence and Traditions of Excellence 

includes a row labeled “History/Multicultural”. Information on this row points out when the national or cultural origins of a piece of music are identified throughout the text. Similarly, Accent on Achievement devotes a row to which “World Music” is included on each page of the student book. 30 

Some books address an introductory letter to the teacher and student that explicitly mentions the connection of music and culture as a desired outcome of study using their methods. For example, the authors of Essential Elements state: “with teaching time in such short supply, it would normally be impractical to take class time to relate music to world cultures… but Essential Elements correlates these activities to the concepts and music throughout the program” (Lautzenheiser et al., 2004, p. 12). Similarly, introductory materials in Accent on Achievement include this statement: “Accent on Achievement … addresses all nine content standards… and provides opportunities to explore relationships between music and the larger culture. Students will learn about the cultural background of musical selections in their book…” (O’Reilly & Williams, 2001, p. 10). The specific use of the words “world cultures”, “culture”, and “cultural” in the introductions to these two texts signals that these books might be used to support a curriculum inclusive of diverse musical practices and contexts that link music to culture. These findings suggest that the authors of each book have created a philosophical position in support of a multicultural music education. None of the books, however, contains a rationale for the inclusion of this multicultural music or how a teacher or student might use the text to learn of the cultural connections of music. No specific student outcome is tied to the study of culturally diverse musical content beyond Accent on Achievement stating that the book allows one to “explore relationships between music and the larger culture” (O’Reilly & Williams, 2001, p. 10). 31 Emergent Theme II: Identity/Ethnicity Labels 

Each publication in this study used labels in both the student and teacher books to denote “provenance” (Brittin & Sheldon, 2004) or the earliest known place of origin for a specific folk song. These labels are justified to the right and located just above the line of music. This is the same location that the name of a composer would typically be printed. The inclusion of the labels in the student books is particularly noteworthy as it serves as a visual cue to mark if a tune originated in a specific culture to the student without relying on the teacher to disclose this information. The labels used in each book are displayed in tables in Appendix A on pages 93 to 97. Combining individual data sets yields interesting findings. Of the five books analyzed in this study, there are 52 different labels used to identify provenance, national identity, or ethnic origins of a specific tune. The national identity referred to the most frequently is “American”. This label is used a total of 50 times throughout the five texts in various iterations such as “American Folk Song”, “American Gospel Hymn”, “American Mountain Song”, and “American Spiritual”. See Appendix A on pages 93 to 97 for a detailed breakdown of how each label is used in each text. Some of the tunes that are labeled as American are published and labeled similarly across various texts analyzed for this study. For example, “Bingo”, “Go Tell Aunt Rhodie”, “Polly Wolly Doodle”, and “Shoo Fly” are printed in three books in this study and “Skip To My Lou” is printed in four. The books analyzed in this study also frequently contain other labels that lack specificity such as “Latin American”, “African”, and “Caribbean”. These labels group 32 

together many diverse peoples and do not indicate any specific provenance, national identity, or culture. For example, the label of “African” refers to the continent of Africa, home to 54 autonomous nations and thousands of discreet indigenous cultures. Such a broad label lacks cultural specificity. “Kum Ba Yah” is labeled as “African” in Accent on Achievement and is accompanied on the page by an illustration of gourds and hand drums. The term “Latin America” is similarly broad. Loosely shared characteristics do exist between the countries typically labeled this way: Romance languages, especially Spanish, are typically spoken – a remnant of colonization by European nations. Standard of Excellence labels the tune “Brother Martin” and Essential Elements labels the tune “La Cucaracha” as “Latin American”. While this term meets the criteria for clearly presented cultural information, it cannot be used to communicate information about a specific group of people. 

Moving beyond labels of culture and nationality, the authors of the books included in this study also label composers. Names of composers were counted as data in this study and grouped into this emergent theme only if the additional context located within the student or teacher book mentioned their nationality or cultural identity. The most acknowledged composers across all combined data sets from this study are Pyotr Il’yich Tchaikovsky, Ludwig van Beethoven, and Stephen Foster. Music written by Tchaikovsky, a Russian-born composer, and Beethoven, a German-born composer, that is arranged throughout the books is most often associated with their instrumental music. Foster was born in the United States and is therefore the most frequently quoted American composer in the books analyzed in this study. 33 

Emergent Theme III: Content Without Context 

Labels of nationality and ethnicity described in the preceding emergent theme help the student and teacher identify musical content connected to various cultures. This content highlights the philosophical positioning of the books included this analysis that claims multicultural connections as a prioritized value. As stated earlier, two of the books explicitly state in an introductory letter that their methods can “relate music to world cultures” (Lautzenheiser et al., 2004, p. 12) and “provide opportunities to explore relationships between music and the larger culture” (O’Reilly & Williams, 2001, p. 10). The other books include information on world music or diverse cultural content in their scope and sequence charts. Therefore, it is important to look specifically at the contexts provided by the method books to teach these relationships. This type of analysis was not completed by Brittin and Sheldon (2004) nor Raponi (2015) and in this study it yielded an interesting dearth of context throughout the books. This lack of context that is explicitly connected to the musical content is reported on in this emergent theme. Aside from the nationality and ethnicity labels, most books give no additional context in the student or teacher book. For example, Accent on Achievement contains 84 pieces of music that met the criteria to be counted as data in this study. No additional information is written in the student book; rather, the authors opt to use illustrations to imply cultural connections. For example, “Mexican Jumping Beans” has a cartoon illustration of dried legumes wearing sombreros and ponchos beside it. “Sakura” is neighbored by an illustration of a cherry blossom tree and a pagoda. “Theme from the 34 

New World Symphony” contains a drawing of ships flying the flag of the American Red Cross. The teacher’s edition contains no additional context because Accent on Achievement publishes a separate Teacher’s Resource Kit that can be purchased for an additional fee. It was therefore not included in this analysis. This supplementary book has duplicable worksheets called “World Music Locators” and are referred to in the teacher’s edition of the method book. 

Essential Elements contains 62 pieces of music that met the criteria to be considered for this study. Only twelve of these pieces include additional information. Nine of those twelve expand on the birthplace of a composer. The other three cover topics such as instruments used in Japanese folk music, the progeny of African-American spirituals, and that the national anthem of Israel was performed by members of the Palestinian Symphony Orchestra. These facts, however, are presented in isolation: additional context is not provided. There is no reference to how instruments are used in Japanese folk music, why spirituals came to be and how they functioned, or why it is worthy to note that the Israeli National Anthem was performed by members of the Palestinian Symphony Orchestra. 

Sound Innovations provides no context related to the multicultural music content in the student book. This is particularly interesting because this method book contained 85 pieces of music that were coded as data for containing cultural information using the labels reported in the previous emergent theme. The teacher’s edition does not expand on contexts, either: rather, it includes instructions to the teacher that they should find recordings of music from various cultures and play it for their students so discussion can 35 

take place. These instructions are included on lines that are labeled as a Mexican Folk Song, Japanese Folk Song, Caribbean Folk Song, and Korean Folk Song. Sound Innovations makes particular use of a label that no other book does: “American Minstrel Song”. No context is provided in the teacher nor student books. Interestingly, the student book version of Standard of Excellence has no context beyond the labeling of the origin of folk songs, but the teacher’s edition contains a significant amount of context. The content available from this text to be coded as data was the highest quantity of any in this study. The data suggest that a large portion of the context is related to geography and language. For example, “find (this country) on a map and speak a phrase in (dominant language of this country)” are pervasive instructions throughout the book. Standard of Excellence provides sample phrases in various languages and includes pronunciations. In total, the countries and regions that students locate and/or speak a phrase in their dominant language are France, Norway, Mexico, the West Indies, Latin America, Australia, China, Africa, Italy, Russia, Wales, Germany, Japan, Scotland, and the Czech Republic. Sometimes half of a page is devoted just to additional cultural contexts, resulting in the music being displaced onto the next page. Of note is information regarding the Aborigine inhabitance and subsequent European colonization of Australia connected to the Australian Folk Song “The Little Fish”, the immense size of Mexico City and the names of Indigenous tribes that thrived in the region alongside the “Mexican Hat Dance”, and a brief history of the division of East and West Germany to be taught with the folk song “Ach! Du Lieber Augustine”. That said, the information given for each culture rarely connects to the music. The context attached 36 

to “Volga Boat Song” depicts Russian mountains and briefly mentions the Cold War. An exception to this is the background on American spirituals included with the tune “Swing Low, Sweet Chariot.” Here, the authors describe the melding of African and American musical traditions, the often unison singing of each spiritual, and the typical thematic material of the lyrics of spirituals. Interestingly, Standard of Excellence does not include a written introduction outlining a value for cultural contexts and relationships. However, these findings demonstrate that this philosophy is indeed present through the information included in the teacher’s edition. 

Traditions of Excellence contains 80 pieces of music that met the criteria to be counted as data in this study. Content is plentiful but context is limited. Most of the additional information is devoted to facts of various composers such as birthplace and what instruments they played. For example, students who use this method book will learn that Stephen Foster was a popular songwriter, Tchaikovsky studied to be a lawyer in Russia, Schop played the violin and trombone in Germany, Handel is considered English but was actually born in Germany, Susato played the trumpet, and Erin Watson plays violin and accordion. The teacher’s edition for Traditions of Excellence merely contains the instructions for each folk song that is labeled by nationality: “Locate (the country) on a world map and share information about the country.” 

Emergent Theme IV: Context Without Critical Thinking 

Many pedagogies for the music classroom – namely comprehensive musicianship (Garofalo, 1983), the national standards (Shuler, Norgaard, & Blakeslee, 2014), culturally 37 

relevant pedagogy (Bond, 2017; Lind & McKoy, 2016) and social justice pedagogies (Gaztambide-Fernández & Rose, 2015; Jorgensen, 2015) – encourage teachers to go beyond musical content and include contextual information that shares stories, makes connections, engages students of all backgrounds, centers diverse epistemologies, and challenges the status quo. Cultural contexts create a narrative for people to learn about something with which they are unfamiliar, challenge assumptions, affirm somebody who is from that culture, and can help accomplish the long-stated goals of a multicultural music education (Anderson, 1991; Arnistine, 1999; Campbell, 2002; Dunbar-Hall, 2005; Elliott, 1995; Hess, 2017). Educators who are not inclined to subscribe to these philosophies still benefit from teaching cultural contexts alongside all their content. As Bradley (2012) states, “without knowledge of context, full meaning [of music] cannot truly be experienced.” As noted in Emergent Theme III, most of the identifiable cultural content that met the criteria to be coded as data in this study was typically not paired with additional contexts for the teacher or student to make connections between various cultures and musics. This lack of context contributes to what Sleeter (2012) deems the marginalization of culturally responsive teaching. However, there is some context that is provided in the method books, and it is therefore important to analyze these data to identify trends between the different books. Educators, publishers, editors, and authors each may individually or collectively interpret the data in this section through their unique philosophies and value systems. 38 

In this emergent theme, I detail a consistent finding across the publications in this study: when context is provided, it is rarely critical in nature. This means that it is usually centered on geography, language, chronology, or cultural artifacts that are considered recall or shallow knowledge. This type of knowledge does not reveal much about the people and their stories. Data included in this emergent theme is sometimes printed in the student book and teacher’s edition as text and sometimes as illustrations. If there were additional steps required to find the data – such as looking at an appendix or a supplementary workbook to be purchased separately – it was not coded as easily identifiable cultural information and therefore excluded from the study. 

Accent on Achievement , along with the illustrations reported earlier, labels “Kookaburra” as an Australian Folk Song. In the additional information provided in the teacher’s edition, teachers learn that the kookaburra is a bird native to Australia. No additional information about Australia, the people, the folk song, or how the folk song came to be is present. Sound Innovations asks students to evaluate their performance for dance style on the music “Mexican Hat Dance” but does not tell us what dance we are emulating or how. Further, the same book labels “Dreydl, Dreydl” as a Traditional Hanukkah Song. The teacher’s edition provides this additional context: “here is a holiday song that uses all of the notes you have learned.” This stands in contrast to Traditions of Excellence , which explains what a dreidel is, how the game is played, what the Hebrew symbols mean, and how that connects to the story of Hanukkah. The location of specific countries is the most common context either provided or instructed to research and teach. Traditions of Excellence asks us to locate on the map 39 

and share information about a specific country 48 times in the teacher’s edition. This sum includes the thirteen times that the country referred to is the United States. The information that gets shared about a country is open-ended since Traditions of Excellence 

does not provide context itself. The teacher’s edition of Standard of Excellence tells us to find 22 countries on the world map and furnishes pictures of the world map in these instructions. Further, context specific to folk songs in this method book often mentions the geography or climate of a region or country where the music was created. For example, folk songs from Wales, Norway, Russia, and Japan all include additional information about mountain ranges. We learn that the West Indies are warm and a desirable vacation destination – one that the authors ask us to imagine visiting during a cold winter – and that Japan experiences heavy rains. Stephen Foster is a complicated figure in music education (Lightweis-Goff, 2008) and is the most frequently published American composer in the books in this study. The lesson learned about Foster through the contexts of the student and teacher books is consistent throughout: he was “America’s first great popular songwriter” (Pearson & Nowlin, 2010, p. 10) who is often called the “father of American music.” (Sheldon et al., 2010, p. 142). No information about the text of his songs, the themes of his work, his intended audience, or the tensions surrounding his legacy are included. This, in a way, reifies a “dangerous single story” (Adichie, 2009) that leads to a critical misunderstanding of the person Stephen Foster, the artist Stephen Foster, and the impact Stephen Foster had on cultures and people outside of the hegemonic norms both historically and presently in our classrooms. 40 

Cultural contexts are sometimes alluded to as the subject of a sentence in the teacher’s editions of the method books, but the information provided connects only to the printed music. Put another way, the authors mention the culture as important context to know but then change subjects immediately. For example, Accent on Achievement 

includes this information for Variation on Lightly Row: “the German tune Lightly Row serves as a basis of creativity by each student creating a variation…” (p. 88) and this context for Amazing Grace: “This American Folk Song’s expressive melody is enhanced by crescendo and decrescendo” (p. 247). Mary Ann is a commonly used folk tune in the books in this study. Accent on Achievement writes “this Jamaican folk song features a review of the tie…” (p. 67) and Sound Innovations prints “this calypso uses your new note” (p. 76). The national and cultural labeling of Jamaican and calypso read as cultural context but, after mentioning it, the authors pivot to musical concepts and do no further exploration of Jamaica, the people, or the calypso as a musical style. Sometimes the context provided for a tune is Eurocentric even if the folk song is labeled as a non-European culture. This functions as cultural context but there is a mismatch between the provenance of the folk song and what is learned. For example, 

Essential Elements labels the name of an American composer – John Higgins – eight times throughout the book. Five of these occurrences are on lines of music that refer to various cultures, i.e., Japanese, Italian, and Latin American. This is the only context provided in four of the five instances in both the student and teacher-facing materials. Further, Accent on Achievement introduces beginning band students to the Korean Folk Song “Arirang”. The student book contains no additional context and the teacher’s 41 

edition tells us that this folk song served as the inspiration for Variations on a Korean Folk Song by American composer John Barnes Chance. This piece is certainly recognized by many band teachers, but students do not get closer to learning of the history or function of this particular folk song by learning this fact. 42 Chapter 5. Discussions 

I have organized the discussions in this chapter to synthesize and build upon findings presented in Chapter IV: Findings. Additional data that did not neatly fit into an emergent theme and are important to share are also included in this chapter to help further illustrate both the explicit and implicit hidden curriculum taught to our beginning band students through the method books. Vallance (1974) explains that hidden curricula are comprised of the “nonacademic but educationally significant consequences of schooling that are not made explicit” (p. 7) but that are still systematically learned by the students. These lessons can relate to morals, social structures, and even relationships of power. Vallance (1974) cautions us to not be too precise about the definition of hidden curriculum: rather, we should embrace the fluidity of the concept to “analyze the phenomenon” (p. 7). Martin (1976) calls researchers to action based on whether we perceive the hidden curriculum to be harmful: if so, then we must root out the “complex set of … practices and structures” (p. 145). Responding to the social injustices and white supremacy in the United States in the year 2021 demands that we critically examine the hidden, implicit curriculum of our beginning band method books. This discussion section, interpreted and created through my lens and position, begins this conversation by linking the cultural labeling practices of five unique publications and interpreting the implicit – and perhaps unintended – narrative created therein. 43 Discussion on Emergent Themes I and III: Philosophical Positioning and Lack of Context 

In Emergent Theme I, I detailed the ways in which books explicitly and implicitly position themselves as supportive of a multicultural music education. Two books contain a letter to music teachers and students claiming that relationships between music and culture are explored in their text. The other three texts include cultural information on their scope and sequence charts. All five books pervasively label the provenance, national identity, or cultural origins of particular folk tunes and contain some amount of context that teaches primarily geography, language, and cultural artifacts. As was pointed out in the previous chapter, however, none of the books in this study provide a rationale for the inclusion of this content and varied amount of context. While the inclusion of country of origin meets the data coding requirement for this study, connections between culture and music are either vague or absent in each book that was analyzed. There does not seem to be a clear reason why information that is printed in the books is there or why it should matter to teachers and students. Further, instructions are redundant or vague. Traditions of Excellence asks students to locate the United States thirteen times, Accent on Achievement includes simple illustrations of cultural artifacts that could be read as stereotypical - such as sombreros and gourds, and Sound Innovations encourages teachers to search out recordings of music from various cultures. 

Essential Elements – a book that explicitly states it can be used to “relate music to world cultures” (p. 12) – uses the least number of cultural labels and provides the least amount of contextual information of any book in the study. Standard of Excellence , while 44 

containing the most context by far of the books in the study, primarily includes information related to location, geography, language, and industry. The redundant and vague instructions, the lack of context, and the type of information detailed throughout the books all intersect with the absence of a rationale for why publishers included this content and how it could be used by teachers and students. Students, teachers, researchers, and the public alike are left without a clear understanding of why certain material is published. The consumers of these materials are left to fill in the gaps in reasoning because of the lack of information on culture, people, contributions, or histories. Why should the information that is included be present at all if nothing besides a rote memorization of facts can be done with it? Does the label describing the origins of a folk tune teach us anything about that song or the culture that produced it? Without this information, it is difficult to identify the motivation to include diverse musical content in each of the books. One might posit that it is because the authors genuinely believe in a philosophy of music education that enhances cultural connections. Another more cynical viewpoint is that multicultural pieces are included as a business decision in reaction to the discourse in the United States pushing for a more diverse and inclusive approach to education. Perhaps this illustrates the idea that perhaps the publishers or authors are including this material to simply say that they included it. If so, this results in a harmful tokenism of cultures that allows books to claim they are inclusive in order to deflect accusations of discrimination. An illusion of diversity is created without addressing any of the root issues for the marginalization of musics in the first place. Teaching musical 45 

content in this way reduces the potential of cultural diversity to simple musical tourism. This musical tourism does not highlight cultural contributions and histories as a way of learning about music and culture more deeply. The contemporary purpose for including music of diverse cultures in curriculum is not rooted in exposure to other cultural artifacts. Instead, teachers and students are advocating for music curricula that tells more complete cultural stories to examine how histories impact current societal inequities and injustices (e.g., Gaztambide-Fernández & Rose, 2015). This includes a sociocultural approach to music education that creates “inquiry-based spaces where learners are invited to discuss, question and interrogate the music experience from different social and cultural positions” (Abril, 2009, p. 77) to make music more realistic and relevant to students’ lives (e.g., Dunbar-Hall, 2005). In including only some surface-level culturally diverse content, the authors of the books are effectively responding to the justifications for a multicultural music education of four decades ago: satiating curiosity of various cultures so that we can all get along with each other (Dodds, 1983). Perhaps the inclusion of this content with little to no meaningful context or clear justification is an example of textbook authors reacting to social pressure while trying to resist politicization. As Apple (1992) states: information in textbooks is never neutral. Mentioning cultural connections and then not teaching cultural connections is innocently misleading at best or a purposefully deceptive marketing tactic at worst. This might seem to the publishers as neutral, but this tepid response to the calls for multicultural music education is still a political stance. Content without context leads to a misunderstanding of the goals of multicultural education pedagogies and further marginalizes these efforts 46 

(Sleeter, 2012). If method books were truly invested in the values of a multicultural music education, then they should deliberately state that and then include the information necessary to teach them. This includes information about actual people – the performance practices and functions of music in the culture, the histories of cultural points of contact, and authentic recordings of the folk songs included in the method books. Sadly, until then, we are left with method books that reduce the potential value of including culturally diverse content in the beginning band curriculum to a form of musical tourism. 

Discussion on Emergent Themes II and IV: Monolithic Labels Without Critical Thought 

Each book in this study indicates cultural content by labeling the provenance of or ethnic culture associated with each folk song. These emergent themes in Chapter IV detailed the name and frequency of the various labels in each method book. The most commonly used labels are “American” and “Traditional”. Neither term is defined in four of the five books. Only Traditions of Excellence defines “Traditional” as the label given to music that has unclear origins (p. 78). That leads us as audience members to ask: what does “American” mean? “Traditional” music from whose perspective? As the method book defines the curriculum of the beginning band classroom (Raponi, 2015), we must consider terms like “American” and how they are used throughout the books in the context of how they have been previously used in curriculum. McCarthy (2015) details the history of music education in the United States – “American” music education – as an enterprise with a “salvationist narrative” and as one 47 

of “cultural imperialism” (p. 34). In the name of uplifting citizens into civility and homogenizing the country through a unifying nationalism, music education in the United States was viewed as an activity that could assimilate immigrants into the dominant language and culture. This Americanization was viewed by the Anglo-American leaders of education as critically important to maintain society. The word “American” was used proudly by music educators throughout the twentieth century to justify both music education’s presence in the schools and the curriculum which deemphasized cultural differences and emphasized American homogeneity. Au, Brown, and Calderón (2016) term this “curricular genocide” (p. 25); a practice by American education erases unique cultural identifiers and assimilates all into the hegemonic epistemologies and values of the dominant culture. They detail examples of “American” curriculum dehumanizing and colonizing Mexican-Americans, Indigenous-Americans, and Chinese-American persons, histories, and knowledges. Acting like a white descendent of Europeans was considered the standard by which other cultures gained access to public education. Speaking English, dressing a certain way, and studying curricula developed with a deficit approach to cultural difference was how various communities were forced to participate in schools and other civic institutions. This resulted in the homogenization and erasure of a significant number of cultural ways of being. These processes were proudly labeled as “American” and set the historical context for how the term “American” is used in curriculum today. The word “American” being used as a description for a homogenizing curriculum does not simply live in the past, though. Recent events reveal ways in which “American” 48 

is used in the present day to quell dissent, erase cultural difference, and invigorate political coalitions who want to see a more unified and standardized curriculum. An example from the last decade illustrates that Arizona, in 2010, outlawed discussions of racial oppression in the classroom in the name of Americanized curriculum (Paris, 2012b). Thirty-one states outlaw bi- and multi-lingual education programs (McCarty & Lee, 2014) in the name of creating a standardized American education system. Even as recently as a few months ago, we see the “American” label being used nefariously in curriculum. The 1776 Report was published January 18, 2021 (The President’s Advisory 1776 Commission, 2021). In the report, the authors promoted an American curriculum that promoted positive stories of the United States and conflated critiques of the United States found in Critical Race Theory and feminism movements with Anti-American censorship. In this way, the authors of the 1776 Report use the word “American” in curriculum to silence dissent and mute cultural differences. It is unclear if the authors of the texts analyzed in this study are aware of the use of the word “American” in general and music curricula throughout history. It is clear after studying the data, though, that “American Folk Song” most regularly refers to a folk song that originated in the United States. The conflation of “American” and “originating in the United States” by the authors erases cultural identities and nuances by grouping people living on two continents and one separate region together: North America, South America, and Central America. But along with being U.S.-centric and assuming use of the label “American” to actually mean “United States”, even a label of “United States” erases cultural difference in this country. Nonspecific and monolithic national labels give 49 

no nuance or cultural context and typically paint a picture of one type of “American”. Because of the melodies that are labeled “American”, this picture of a musical American is of a person who speaks English and is of European descent. Perhaps the authors of books can choose labels that are more specific. For example, Standard of Excellence uses the label “American Mountain Song”, Sound Innovations uses the label “American Gospel Hymn”, and Essential Elements uses the label “African-American Spiritual”. This type of labeling is more nuanced and accompanying context in the books could refer to who originated the folk song and in which part of the United States they resided at the time. Even further, the authors of the books could use terms like “Appalachian”, “Chicano”, or “Lakota Tribe” to refer to geographic regions and groups of people. Labeling in this way honors differences between discrete groups of people, denotes cultural contributions to the diversity of the United States, and allows for more detailed approaches to teaching multicultural music in a beginning band classroom. Relatedly, the most referenced composer born in the United States throughout the books in this study is Stephen Foster. Stephen Foster has come under recent scrutiny (Lightweis-Goff, 2008) and his story is complicated. Some of his songs were written explicitly for performance in minstrel shows. These shows were performed by white actors who would paint their skin black and speak in dialects that poked fun at the way in which recently freed enslaved peoples or other African Americans spoke. The lyrics often painted a picture of idyllic plantation and slave life meant to comedically entertain white audiences. Some of his most famous tunes written for minstrel shows are “Camptown Races” and “Oh! Susanna”. Oh! Susanna is printed in Sound Innovations and Essential 50 

Elements . Camptown Races is printed in Accent on Achievement, Sound Innovations, Traditions of Excellence , and Essential Elements . Stephen Foster is labeled as the composer in all of the above circumstances. The authors of Sound Innovations are aware of this history: they label a tune, “The Blue-Tail Fly”, as an American Minstrel Tune (Sheldon et al., 2010, p. 315). I would like to combine data from all the individual books again to pose two final questions as discussion points to this emergent theme. The most frequently used national label in the books in this study is “American”, the most frequently used non-cultural label in the books in this study is “Traditional”, and the most frequently referenced composer who was born in the United States is Stephen Foster. The tunes in the books that are credited to Stephen Foster were written for use in blackface minstrelsy shows. So, what narrative is to be interpreted here? How does this intersect with the first and third emergent themes that detail how books include cultural content but no contexts or rationale for teaching it? 

(dis)Honorable Mentions 

This portion of the chapter details some of the data from individual data sets that did not fit neatly into an emergent theme and was not prevalent enough among the books to be an emergent theme itself. 

Language and the Hidden Curriculum 51 

Analysis of the contextual information yielded findings related to the adjectives used and instructions given for specific types of folk music or other cultural content throughout the student and teacher books. These findings were not generalizable as they were contained locally to the teacher’s edition data sets for Accent on Achievement and 

Sound Innovations .The teacher’s edition books for Accent on Achievement and Sound Innovations 

use the words “famous”, “familiar”, and “popular” when describing some of the folk music in the book. For example, the melodies “Long, Long Ago”, “Frere Jacques”, “William Tell”, and “It’s Raining, It’s Pouring” are all described as “familiar” by the authors of Sound Innovations . There is some overlap with Accent on Achievement , where these authors label “Hot Cross Buns”, “Au Claire de la Lune”, “Surprise Symphony”, “Finale from Orpheus”, and “William Tell Overture” with the words “famous” or “popular”. It is important to note that the words famous, familiar, and popular are all subjective and broad; what is the threshold a song must pass in order to be labeled this way? And, more importantly to this study, who is the audience who describes these tunes as famous, familiar, or popular? There is one thing that all of these tunes have in common: they are all Eurocentric. The use of these adjectives by these books further centers – albeit subtly and not immediately made clear – the expectation that the students and/or teachers are white descendants of Europeans. In stark contrast, Sound Innovations 

describes the instruments used in a Japanese Folk Song as “unusual” and the melody of an Arabic Folk Song as “exotic”. Vallance (1974) argues that this hidden curriculum, though, is still learned systematically even if not explicitly taught. 52 

Another instance of language creating a hidden curriculum is present in Sound Innovations . Line 109 in the student book is the tune “Michael, Row Your Boat Ashore” and it is labeled “African-American Spiritual” by the authors. The student book includes an instruction unique to this line of music that is not printed anywhere else in the book: “always play with a beautiful sound” (Sheldon et al., 2010, p. 204). It is curious and most likely entirely innocent that this instruction was printed on the only line in the book that is explicitly labeled by the authors as a piece of music created by African-Americans. However, the pairing of this instruction on this line gives the impression that, were we to play this song in the style suggested in the title, we might not be playing with “beautiful sound”. This placement becomes less innocent, though, when the rest of the context is illustrated. Recall that Sound Innovations uses the term “American” more than any other book in this study and refers to Stephen Foster more than any other book in this study. In fact, Line 174, “The Blue-Tail Fly”, is explicitly labeled by the authors as an American Minstrel Tune. Perhaps a glaring oversight occurred on the part of the editors, but the implied narrative of these data all taken together is that this book is engaging deliberately in upholding white American supremacy. 

Uniformity of Content. 

Noticeable throughout all of the books in this study was a uniformity of the content. I label and interpret this to mean pieces of music or folk tunes that are printed in at least three of the five publications. For a chart of songs meeting this criteria and which books they are published in, see Appendix B on page 98. This phenomenon is worthy of 53 

discussion through the lens of multiculturalism. A common argument against changing the content in a curriculum is that there is not enough space for new content. Rather, this finding demonstrates that so much of the content is redundant among various method books. Instead, teachers, authors, and/or publishers could replace some of this preexisting content with diverse content and informational and educational contexts. For example, after a concept is introduced there are typically a few pieces of music that apply that concept in various iterations. These spaces are opportunities for authors to include multicultural musical content that differentiates their books from the other books currently on the market. 54 Chapter 6. Implications, Limitations, and Recommendations for Further Research 

In this paper, I outlined two literature bases that establish a long history of advocacy for a multicultural music education curriculum and how this curriculum has previously been analyzed, interpreted, and interrogated. The beginning band method book often defines the curriculum of the beginning band classroom and has therefore been studied many times. Previous analyses focused primarily on the pedagogical content (e.g., Byo, 1988; Robinson, 1980; Tullberg, 1992) and philosophical values (e.g., Heavner, 1995; Morris, 2000; Paschall, 2006) of each text, but have only recently scrutinized how culture is represented throughout the pages (Brittin & Sheldon, 2004; Raponi, 2015). This reflects the growing frequency and intensity with which the music education profession is calling for meaningful change to our practices, pedagogies, and content to become more culturally responsive and inclusive (Abril, 2006; Bond, 2017; Hess, 2017). The previous studies on cultural representation in beginning band method books, however, simply quantified which cultures were labeled throughout the books and the frequency with which they were presented. This present study similarly quantified which cultures were labeled and the frequency of each label, but also analyzed the contextual information regarding culture that is present in the student and teacher editions of these books. These findings were reported through four emergent themes: 55 

philosophical positioning, labels of national identity or ethnicity, content without context, and context without critical thinking. I followed the findings with discussions reflective of living and teaching music in the United States in 2021. So now, the questions must be asked: why does this matter? Why is this so important right now, in the United States, in 2021? Can we do different? Can we do better? Can we do different, better? I address these questions in this chapter. Recommendations for the profession and ideas for future research are shared as well. 

Why does this matter? 

Elliott (1995) reminds us that music is a diverse “artistic, social, and cultural” practice (p. 198). A quality music education, therefore, is one that thoroughly integrates varying ideologies, cultural backgrounds, and histories together in an aesthetically and socially meaningful way. Diversity is acknowledged, appreciated, and sustained by listening to, learning about, performing, responding to, and creating diverse musical content and contexts. If a democratic aim of education is to produce a balanced and equitable society (Dewey, 1923), then this multicultural integration is necessary. As our democracy becomes more diverse, students must be aware of and produce knowledge and skills that reflect this value. Music education, as a cultural and humanistic education, is therefore one that invites students to critique and ask questions about our cultural histories to create balanced and equitable cultural futures. But our school band programs do not reflect the cultural, racial, and socioeconomic demographics of our schools. As Elpus and Abril (2019) point out, white 56 

students and students from high socioeconomic backgrounds are dramatically overrepresented in the enrollment data. Black students, Hispanic students, and students living in poverty are as equally underrepresented in the enrollment data. Thorough integration of diverse cultures is certainly made more challenging in a band program that may appeal more to richer and whiter students. Music educators concerned with this figure examine financial barriers of instrumental music programs as a possible culprit. We know that schools with a higher population of traditionally minoritized communities do not receive as equitable funding as their whiter counterparts (Education Trust, 2005; Ladson-Billings, 2006) and this is true for band programs as well (Costa-Giomi & Chappell, 2007). Teachers must raise funds and cut additional fees to attract students who traditionally have not participated in school band programs because of financial barriers to ensure an equitable school music experience. However, lack of diversity in curriculum is another barrier that pushes students not to participate in or simply elect out of participation in various activities (e.g., San Pedro, 2018). We know that academic achievement is a predictor for minoritized students’ decisions to enroll and continue in music programs (Kinney, 2010, 2019) and that academic achievement is significantly improved when the students participate in a curriculum that is responsive to and sustaining of their cultures (Ladson-Billings, 1995; Paris, 2012). The traditionally Eurocentric curriculum of beginning band classes (Raponi, 2015) marginalizes students of color and therefore inverts the ideals of an education in a democracy (Dewey, 1923). The music education profession collectively has pushed for 57 

more diverse content and pedagogies for almost a century. Various historical rationales for this philosophy include helping students to learn to live together to combat stereotypes (Anderson, 1991), enhancing students’ regards of others so they may interact more effectively (Arnistine, 2000), and connecting students “with the personhood of other musicers and audiences in other times and places” (Elliott, 1995, p. 209). More contemporary justifications for a multicultural music education relate to the point outlined in this brief section: the central concern of music education is transmitting musical traditions from one generation to the next (Jorgensen, 2015), musical values can foster “the types of social democratic behaviors desirable for broader public participation and engagement” (Westheimer, 2015, p. 108), and a culturally diverse curriculum embraces the needs and interests of students from “diverse racial, ethnic, social class, and cultural communities.” (Campbell, 2015, p. 273). Ultimately, as Hess (2017) states: “when we engage students’ own music interests and experiences in the classroom, we communicate powerfully to students that their perspectives (and their musics) are valued and valuable” (p. 73). This justification assumes the opposite to be true as well: when we do not engage more culturally diverse musical content, we are implying these are not valuable musics or peoples worthy of formal study in a school setting. This present analysis matters because it allows the profession to reckon first with what is so that we can, if desired, imagine and act on what could be. This does not need to result in a radical shift or even a pause of instrumental music; rather, it is a valuable opportunity for needed critical self-reflection on our pedagogies, content, and the overt and covert narratives communicated to our students through our curriculum. This 58 

research establishes a baseline from which other interpretations, recommendations, and inquiries may flow. If beginning band teachers are interested in opening the curriculum so that diverse musical content and the stories told about that content are more meaningful and impactful, then a logical place to make adjustments is the beginning band method book. 

Why is this important right now – in 2021? 

NAEP data from 2019 shows that the “achievement gap” between white students and students of color is the largest it has ever been (The Nation’s Report Card, 2019). Inequality in society in the United States is growing and our education system has not been successful at disrupting this pattern (Ladson-Billings, 2006). Franklenberg, Lee, and Orfield (2003) reported that America’s public schools were more than a decade into a process of resegregation. Nearly three-fourths of Black and Latinx students attend schools that are predominantly students of color. This trend has continued into the present-day; as neighborhoods become slightly less segregated, school choice has allowed the pattern of resegregation in public schools to continue and even expand in many places (Owens, 2020; Wells, Keener, Cabral, & Cordova-Cobo, 2919). 

As mentioned before, our music programs do not, overall, reflect the demographics of students who attend schools in the United States (Elpus & Abril, 2019). Advocacies for more culturally responsive pedagogies that engage students in analyzing information through the lens of the worlds they interpret and experience continue to grow. These pedagogies – culturally relevant pedagogy (Abril, 2013; Bond, 2017; Lind & 59 

McKoy, 2016) and social justice pedagogies (Gaztambide-Fernández & Rose, 2015; Jorgensen, 2015) - encourage teachers to go beyond musical content and include contextual information that shares stories, makes connections, engages students of all backgrounds, centers diverse epistemologies, and challenges the status quo. They ask us to not just include content and context but create environments where truly critical thinking (Shaw, 2014) is the norm and stereotypes are challenged. These approaches have well-documented success in raising the academic achievement of students of color in the general education literature (Cummins, 1986; Ladson-Billings, 1995; Ladson-Billings, 2006). Curriculum in 2021 is an ethical decision; what information and whose stories should get transmitted to the next generation? Whose interpretations and experiences should be valued? Should schools serve as sites for social reproduction (Gutmann, 1999) or as sites for envisioning a more equitable society for all? If the purpose of our schools is to build a balanced society (Dewey, 1923), then in every class the content we teach, stories we tell, and questions we ask must be diverse and inclusive. Perhaps then our education system will begin paying down historical education debts (Ladson-Billings, 2006) and assist in rebuilding a more equitable society for all residents in the United States. 

What can teachers of beginning band do? 

The importance of teacher autonomy in determining which method book to use in their beginning band curriculum cannot be overstated. Since music is a subject that is not 60 

standardized and does not have high-stakes assessments tied to it, teachers of beginning band are most often the sole decision-makers when determining what to teach in their classrooms. There are many different method books available for purchase and the findings from this research outline what multicultural content and context is contained within five of the most popular texts. Teachers need to weigh their philosophical values when choosing a method book; how important is multicultural content to them, their students, and their communities? This value is also in conversation with how each text presents and reinforces various musical concepts (Byo, 1988; Tullberg, 1992), has additional online resources for students to explore (McDannald, 2012), and connects to national standards (Watkins, 2011). Ultimately, teachers must select the method book that balances these values the best for their students and communities. Findings reported here show that beginning band method books include varying degrees of multicultural content and varying depths of information about the music and people. Regardless of the book that they choose, teachers who are diligently working towards a more diverse and inclusive curriculum can highlight specifically how the provenance of a folk song is labeled in each book and determine if the context in the student and teacher books are sufficient. If they decide to supplement the information, then there are a few simple ways that they can seek out additional context. A tenet of culturally responsive (Ladson-Billings, 1995; Lind & McKoy, 2016) and culturally sustaining (Paris, 2012) pedagogies are honoring and including student expertise and epistemologies in the classroom. This means that beginning band teachers can lean on students who may have experience outside of the schools with various styles 61 

and genres of music to share both pedagogical information about music performance and about how music functions in a given group of people. Further, cross-curricular connections are advocated by the national standards for music (Shuler, Norgaard, & Blakeslee, 2014). Teachers of beginning band can involve the social studies teachers on campus to develop curriculum that enhances and builds on prior knowledge. For example, if students in band are learning the African-American spiritual, “Michael Row Your Boat Ashore”, then the information shared in band can echo and build on information taught in social studies about the role and function of religion and music in communities of previously enslaved peoples. Finally, we can use the scope and sequence charts to our advantage to analyze what musical concepts or skills are taught or reinforced on a specific line of music regardless of cultural representation. If the beginning band teacher has decided to include more diverse content in their class, they can quickly arrange or rote-teach a folk song that teaches or reinforces the same musical concepts or skills as a preexisting line of music in the book. For example, I previously taught two students in beginning band who had recently emigrated to the United States from Guyana. A popular Guyanese folk song, Kuma-Kuma Fish, uses eighth notes and the syncopated rhythm of one eighth note followed by one quarter note followed by one eighth note. The range of the melody is a perfect fourth. Instead of using the contrived line in the book that taught and reinforced this rhythm, I quickly wrote out the melody Kuma-Kuma Fish and displayed it on the projector for the class to learn. The Guyanese students – who I knew from previous interactions were excited and enthusiastic to share their culture and experience it in a school setting – were engaged and volunteered to 62 

teach the band a rhythmic accompaniment that could be performed alongside the folk song. It is important to remember, though, that when we teach Eurocentric music without context and styles of music from outside of Europe with context, we can be deploying a hidden curriculum (Vallance, 1980) that assumes and normalizes Eurocentric ideals as universal. The absence of additional context creates an assumption that prior knowledge should already include information about a given culture. The content in our beginning band method books that is representative of a certain culture should be taught with additional context – including the music that derives from European techniques or peoples. This helps de-normalize whiteness, centers diverse experiences and knowledges, and helps students experience music more fully (Bradley, 2012). 

Recommendations for Music Teacher Educators 

Considering the increased demand from teachers and researchers to include culturally diverse content in the school music classroom, music teacher educators may need to reexamine how their preservice music educators experience these conversations throughout their degree programs. As Gay (2005) notes, teacher preparation programs are “typically designed to prepare middle-class, European American candidates to teach middle-class, European American students in mainstream schools” (p. 222). Since the school music programs in the United States are even whiter and richer than the typical school demographics (Elpus & Abril, 2019), it is possible that the music education teacher candidates are even more disproportionately white than the general education 63 

teacher candidates that Gay (2005) mentioned. Conversations and open discussions about cultural diversity and inclusion need to happen with these students. These discussions should happen regularly throughout the curriculum and not be sidelined or Othered (Gay, 2005). Music teacher educators need to model the selection of culturally diverse content and responsive pedagogies in their own practices so that preservice music teachers experience it firsthand rather than simply read and talk about these pedagogies in theory. These preservice music educators should also have the practice of teaching in a culturally-responsive way as a normalized technique prior to entering the classroom. The points I make above are problematized, though, by the audition and selection procedures that determine if a student is eligible to become a music major in the first place. Koza (2008) makes the claim that a successful audition into a music degree program requires previous access to privilege. Royston and Springer (2017) report that applied private lessons faculty often make the final decisions whether or not to admit a study into a music major. Often, these professors prioritize high school grade point averages, present performance abilities, or subjective traits like teachability. While these concerns are well outside the scope of this paper, the implications of how music teacher educators can take the findings from this paper into their music education programs are indeed complicated by the demography of music education programs. 

Can we do different, better? 

Teachers of beginning band both define their curriculum using the method book and are constrained by what content and contexts are present in the method book. 64 

Advocacy for the inclusion of diverse content in this curriculum has occurred for over one century and has been carried out by leaders of the music education profession at the national level and in-service teachers. Rationales have shifted from creating a unified nation in the middle of the twentieth century, to helping peoples of various backgrounds get along with each other in the late twentieth century, to the contemporary justifications that focus on sustaining cultural identity and working to end the replication of social injustices. Findings from this study show that five popular and easily accessible beginning band method books do include a variety of diverse content, but the most frequent provenance of folk songs are the United States and western Europe. The authors of the texts do not frequently include context that promotes critical thinking. We – researchers and in-service teachers – should continue to interrogate why authors of method books are using outdated justifications for the inclusion of multicultural music. A short-term result of these inquiries may lead to teachers purchasing method books that are more aligned with their multicultural philosophies. In the long-term, publishers may gauge a shift in the demand for their books due to the presence of or lack of cultural content and they may invite their authors and editors to write an update that includes more of this material. It must be acknowledged that publishers’ decisions are constrained by basic economics. They create more of what sells and earns a profit. Editing and overhauling entire method books are monumental tasks that require significant time, energy, and finances. I do not intend to paint a negative image of book authors, editors, and publishers in this study or misrepresent their intentions. However, as discussed in 65 

Emergent Theme I, we do not know of their intentions or rationales for included multicultural musical content because they do not include this information in the book. Ultimately, the job of the authors and publishers is to make a product that is palatable for an incredibly diverse audience. This includes teachers and students in predominantly white spaces and in traditionally minoritized spaces. This audience includes teachers and students who want to avoid politics and those who consider teaching an overtly political act. It includes schools where band enrollment is smaller than ten students and schools where band enrollment is larger than 400 students. However, because method books are so popular and have such a wide reach, they also have a lot of influence. Teachers typically supplement the method books with additional information, but if culturally diverse content was to be easily accessible within the method book this would make teaching easier for the rapidly growing population of music educators who want to be more culturally responsive in their curricula. Teachers of beginning band who supplement their curriculum with diverse content can share best practices, present clinics, and write articles in journals popular amongst in-service teachers to continue to advocate for more robust change. It is noteworthy that much celebrated curriculum reform has happened in the music textbooks used in the elementary schools (Campbell, 2002) but not so much in the beginning band method books. This creates a disconnect in what musical experiences and worlds students participate in in elementary school to what they experience in middle school. Middle school teachers – specifically those who teach beginning band – can demonstrate to their colleagues that curricular revision is possible and that their students and programs are 66 

better for it. If these beginning band teachers want to move their curricula in this direction but are unsure, they can continue to pressure state organizations to host professional development clinics on these topics. Like-minded teachers of beginning band might similarly establish their own groups on social media platforms to share ideas, struggles, and successes. Perhaps a reasonable first step can be to involve the publishers’ voices in research like this. There was a lot of information open to interpretation throughout this study because the terms and philosophies printed throughout the texts were not clearly defined by the authors. Curious researchers and teachers might ask publishers, editors, and authors why they include multicultural content. This would help trace how this now-clearly stated value system impacts the content and context present or absent in the book(s). A replicated analysis with this information might yield some additional interesting findings and spark new discussions. It might also open a policy window where teachers and publishers can work together to create a curriculum that is more inclusive, tells more complete stories, and asks more critical questions. 

Limitations and Recommendations for Further Research 

The role of the teacher is critical in determining if these multicultural contents and contexts get shared and how the students engage with them. Therefore, the teacher and their philosophical values is a limitation in this study. Music inhabits a gray area in education policy: it is a mandated subject of study in the elementary level and is an elected activity in secondary schools in many states. Recent publications state that 94% 67 

of elementary schools (Parsad & Spiegelman, 2012) and 74% of high schools in the United States (Elpus, 2020) offer music instruction. Other investigations specifically on charter schools report significantly lower availability of music programs (Hedgecoth, 2017, 2020). Some states require a credit of fine arts for graduation from high school but implementations of this mandate vary widely (Arts Education Partnership, 2019). While many music subject assessments were developed in the last decade, no high-stakes consequences are attached to student performance on these tests. Put another way, a student who participates in a music class but fails any test attached to that course does not have to repeat a grade. There are national and state standards for instrumental music, but band specifically is not a standardized subject with a uniform curriculum. A large degree of curricular autonomy is afforded to the teacher who ultimately decides what to teach. Once the teacher decides what music they will use to define their curriculum (Reynolds, 2000), they then have the freedom to choose what information about each piece of music to transmit to students. Method books that include a significant amount of context in the teacher’s edition place the responsibility of sharing cultural information on the teacher. Method books that include limited cultural contexts in the student books rely on the student being curious to search for more information. For this, we must consider and interpret the findings of this research in a setting where the teacher decides whether the cultural information is shared, expanded upon, or ignored. An imaginary method book that includes diverse musical content and inclusive, thorough contexts can only be brought to life through the decisions and actions made by the teacher in the band room. 68 

A critical assumption that beginning band teachers value culturally diverse content was made in forming the need for this study. This assumption also functions as a limitation to this study. A crucial question must be asked of currently practicing teachers of beginning band in future research: does cultural representation matter when selecting a method book? Does it matter to students? If not, should it? Further, we know empirically that teachers may state a set of values but that occasionally teachers struggle to employ pedagogies and select content reflective of these philosophies. Interviews with and observations of various beginning band teachers could determine how the cultural content and context of method books is being used in the classroom, how this information is valued by teachers, and what suggestions they have to make method books more diverse. This research establishes an academic baseline of what cultural content and contexts are present in five popular and easily accessible beginning band method books using basic quantitative and qualitative methodologies. Future research can include more detailed examinations of how cultures are defined discursively throughout the texts – especially the most frequently used labels such as “American” and “Traditional”. A musicological analysis could study the history and function of each folk song in its original form to understand more about how the content of the method books creates various narratives that are taught explicitly or learned implicitly. It would be interesting to examine various method books historically to uncover when – and perhaps why – specific tunes became this common in beginning band method books. 69 Conclusion 

A limitation to this study acknowledged the role of the teacher in conjunction with the gray area of education policy that music inhabits. I view this another and more optimistic way, too; if music is not a standardized subject and teachers control the curriculum, then what limits us? What is preventing teachers from creating a more culturally responsive curriculum that is unique to their communities? Let us empower each other to think critically about the children we teach and what should be taught in a public and democratic education system. We must not be burdened and constrained by the centuries-old tradition of a utilitarian view of music education and band (Allsup & Benedict, 2008); one that historically emphasized discipline and order (Jorgensen, 1994) and Eurocentrism (McCarthy, 2015). After all, evolutions in justifications for why school music matters have occurred many times. The words of Langer, Reimer, Gardner, and Elliott all pushed the collective profession to consider how music functions in society and asked us to envision a new future: one that was more artistic, aesthetic, intelligent, and praxial. Teachers of beginning band play a crucial role in the new direction of music education as the initial instrumental instruction in a student’s life. Findings from this study, though, illustrate that beginning band method books indeed do constrain teachers from easily developing a curriculum that is more diverse and thoroughly inclusive. This research analyzed five popular and easily accessible beginning band method books to answer research questions about how culture is represented and what cultural contexts are presented throughout the pages of the student and teacher’s editions. It was determined and reported through four emergent themes that: the books in 70 

this study explicitly and implicitly positioned themselves as supportive of a multicultural music education but did not include rationales and justifications for those choices; to denote cultural information, books use a system of labels that identify provenance or national origin of a given folk song or composer; much of this multicultural content lacks additional context or information; and when there is context in the student and teacher books, it is most often trivial information about geography, climate, and language that does not include critical learning or thinking about the culture or the role of music in that culture. These findings were discussed through the contemporary lens of society in the United States in 2021. Residents of the United States are experiencing dual pandemics: one is a prolonged public health crisis and the other is the impact of long-existing systemic inequities and racism on BIPOC. Schools are reproducing these inequalities rather than disrupting them. Scholars note that standardized curricula have only widened the achievement gap between learners of various demographics (Sleeter, 2012). Teachers must reform curricula to create more thorough integration of diverse cultures. Our methodologies must be more culturally responsive – for if they are not, this, too, is another barrier constructed to equal access. This all starts with more diverse and inclusive content. As the music education profession reckons with the roles we play in excluding certain groups of students from our classes, debate has grown over the apolitical methods advocated by some and the social justice pedagogies advocated by others. Those in favor of a more culturally diverse and responsive curriculum point out that having a neutral 71 

political stance regarding this topic is actually a stance in favor of the status quo. Recommendations for further research presented in this paper proposed including a diverse sample of practicing beginning band teachers’ voices in these debates and how their thoughts intersect with the curriculum present in beginning band method books. Music must be a leader not just in desegregating our schools once again but also in thoroughly integrating our students, cultures, and communities. I think this is possible. I think this is possible in general music classes and I think this is possible in large ensemble classes like beginning band. Beginning band method books are an important tool in this work. If we, as a profession, find them to be deficient then we can and must advocate for change. Must we follow or can we lead? I believe we can lead – and we can lead now. 72 References Abril, C. R.
